1.title: God Established Marriage: The Designer of Marriage

mem.t: Therefore a man will leave his father and his mother, and will join with his wife, and they will be one flesh.

s: Look through your wedding photos or wedding video together, and each share the one moment from that day you remember most.
Take turns finishing this sentence: “I thank God for bringing you into my life, because...”
Read Genesis 2:24 together, then hold hands and pray: “Lord, you established our marriage. Please be the Lord of our home.”

lessons.title: Who Designed Marriage?
lessons.theme: Marriage is God’s invention, not ours

v: God created man in his own image. In God’s image he created him; male and female he created them.

God blessed them. God said to them, “Be fruitful, multiply, fill the earth, and subdue it. Have dominion over the fish of the sea, over the birds of the sky, and over every living thing that moves on the earth.”
Unless the LORD builds the house, they who build it labor in vain. Unless the LORD watches over the city, the watchman guards it in vain.

lessons.still: Be still and take a deep breath. Tell the Lord: “Lord, you designed my marriage, and today I want to come back to your blueprint.” Gently lay your weariness and disappointment before him.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Marriages often run into trouble because we want to be the designer ourselves, making our own rules and calling our own shots. To return to our rightful place is to admit that God is the Lord of marriage and I am his steward. Let people be people, and let God be God, and the home will find true security.
lessons.jesus: When Jesus was asked about marriage, he didn’t quote the rabbis’ debates of his day. He pointed to “he who made them from the beginning” (Matthew 19:4), leading people back to God’s original design. Jesus is our example: when marriage gets hard, we go back to God’s heart first, not to human methods.
lessons.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for establishing marriage and for blessing husband and wife from the very beginning. We admit that we often want to be in charge and run this home our own way. Today we give our marriage back to you. Please be the designer of our home and its builder too. In the name of the Lord Jesus, amen.
teach: When you buy a new appliance, the most reliable manual always comes from the factory that designed it, not from a neighbor’s experience. Marriage is the same. Our culture hands us plenty of marriage “manuals”: advice from the internet, patterns from the families we grew up in, our own feelings. But marriage was not invented by people; it was established by God, and the most accurate manual is found in the Bible.

Right at the start, Genesis tells us: “In God’s image he created him; male and female he created them” (Genesis 1:27), and then “God blessed them” (Genesis 1:28). Marriage existed before sin ever entered the world. It is not a repair job after the fall; it is God’s good original design, and it carries his blessing. Husband and wife together bear God’s image: different from each other, yet equal in dignity.

The psalmist says: “Unless the LORD builds the house, they who build it labor in vain” (Psalm 127:1). Many couples work very hard: working to earn money, working to communicate, working to be patient, and they grow more and more exhausted. The problem is not a lack of effort; it is a question of who the builder is. When God is both the designer and the builder, our effort is not wasted. Change your mindset and your life will change: our marriage is, first of all, God’s handiwork.
q: How much of my current view of marriage comes from my family of origin, from society, or from my own feelings, rather than from the Bible?
In our home, is there an area where I keep wanting to be the “designer”?
talk: Before we married, what did you most look forward to in marriage? How has that expectation changed?
If our marriage were a house, which part do you think most needs God to rebuild?
acts: Say to your spouse today: “Thank you for building this home with me.”
Write down one area of family life you want to hand back to God’s leadership
Before bed, pray one sentence for your spouse: “Lord, please build him/her up.”
lessons.noon: “Unless the LORD builds the house, they who build it labor in vain” — Lord, right now I lay down my own methods. Please build our home.

lessons.title: Leaving: The Start of a New Home
lessons.theme: We leave our parents to set new priorities

v: Therefore a man will leave his father and his mother, and will join with his wife, and they will be one flesh.
“For this cause a man will leave his father and mother and will be joined to his wife. Then the two will become one flesh.”

lessons.still: Close your eyes and picture the step you took out of your parents’ home on your wedding day. Quietly ask the Lord: “Lord, are there places in my heart that still haven’t truly ‘left’?”
lessons.light: 321 Light: True leaving starts with leaving the old self-centered life. The patterns of our family of origin are so hard to change because they have long since become part of my “self.” Only when we let Jesus reign will old habits be replaced by new life.
lessons.jesus: At twelve, Jesus said: “Didn’t you know that I must be in my Father’s house?” (Luke 2:49). He honored his earthly parents and obeyed them, yet he knew clearly that his highest priority was his heavenly Father. Jesus shows us that honoring parents and having the right priorities can go together.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for our parents, and thank you for building a new home for us. Help us honor our parents while truly putting each other first. Wherever patterns from our families of origin don’t please you, heal and renew us, and let your word become the standard for our home. Amen.
teach: Genesis 2:24 is the Bible’s most-quoted verse on marriage; both Jesus and Paul quote it. The verse contains three actions: leave, join, and become one flesh. The order matters. It’s like building a house: first you clear the foundation, then you raise the pillars, and finally you put on the roof. Today we look at the first action: leaving.

To “leave his father and his mother” (Genesis 2:24) is not disrespect, and it doesn’t mean cutting off the relationship. It means a change of priorities. Before marriage, my most important relationship was with the family I grew up in; after marriage, my spouse becomes my first priority among all earthly relationships. Much of the tension in marriage comes not from a lack of love but from one partner’s heart not having left yet: still asking parents first about big decisions, still running home to Mom to complain after getting hurt.

Leaving also happens on the inside: leaving behind the old patterns of our family of origin. For example, my father always showed displeasure through silence, so I give my spouse the cold shoulder; my mother always nagged, so without realizing it I nag to show I care. Leaving means letting Scripture, not my family of origin, become the standard for our home.
q: Which pattern from my family of origin is affecting our marriage right now?
When I face a decision or feel hurt, who is the first person I think of?
talk: In what ways do you think I’ve already “left” well? Where do I still need to grow? Please say it gently.
What good traditions did each of us bring from our families that we want to keep?
acts: Write down one old pattern from your family of origin that you want to “leave”
When a decision comes up today, talk it over with your spouse first
Pray once for each set of parents, asking God to bless them
lessons.noon: “a man will leave his father and his mother, and will join with his wife” — Lord, right now I put my spouse back in the place of priority you’ve given us.

lessons.title: Joining: The Glue of Commitment
lessons.theme: Joining is choosing every day to hold fast to each other

v: Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their labor.
For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow; but woe to him who is alone when he falls, and doesn’t have another to lift him up.
Again, if two lie together, then they have warmth; but how can one keep warm alone?
If a man prevails against one who is alone, two shall withstand him; and a threefold cord is not quickly broken.

lessons.still: Gently clasp your hands together and feel your palms pressing against each other. Tell the Lord: “Lord, bind our hearts together just as tightly, and be the one who holds us together in the middle.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: The self-ruled heart only wants to be lifted up, kept warm, and protected; the self-emptied heart asks first, “How can I lift you up?” Joining isn’t demanding that my spouse cling to me; it’s me laying myself down first, for Jesus and for my spouse.
lessons.jesus: God promises: “I will in no way leave you, neither will I in any way forsake you” (Hebrews 13:5). We see this heart all through Jesus’ life: when the disciples were weak, ran away, and denied him, he still sought them out and restored them. Jesus’ commitment doesn’t rest on our reliability, but on his faithfulness.
lessons.pray: Faithful Lord, thank you for never leaving us. Be the third strand of our marriage. When we are weak, weary, and tempted to let go, bind us tightly together with your love. And teach us to lift each other up first, rather than only waiting to be lifted up. Amen.
teach: The original word for “join” carries the sense of “sticking to, clinging tightly,” like two sheets of paper glued together: if you force them apart, both sheets tear. The marriage God designed is not “living together for a while” but one life bonded to another. That also explains why divorce wounds people so deeply: what is torn apart is two lives that had become bonded.

The Teacher says: “Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their labor” (Ecclesiastes 4:9). To be joined means someone lifts you up when you fall, someone keeps you warm when you’re cold, someone stands with you when you’re attacked. Joining is not a feeling; it is a choice repeated every day: today I still choose to stand on your side.

The most beautiful line is the last one: “a threefold cord is not quickly broken” (Ecclesiastes 4:12). However strong two strands are, life can still wear them through. But when God becomes the third strand, a marriage gains a resilience beyond human strength. So the best way for a couple to be joined is not only to move closer to each other, but to move closer to God together.
q: In our marriage, am I more often the one who lifts up, or the one waiting to be lifted up?
Has anything happened lately that makes me want to step back and not hold on so tightly?
talk: Think back to a hard time we went through together. What kept us from falling apart then?
When have you most needed me to stand on your side lately?
acts: Take the initiative today and ask your spouse: “Is there anything I can help carry for you?”
Give your spouse a hug that lasts ten seconds
Write down one grace God gave you as you got through a hard time together, and post it somewhere visible at home
lessons.noon: “a threefold cord is not quickly broken” — Lord Jesus, right now please be the strand that binds us together.

lessons.title: One Flesh: No Longer Two
lessons.theme: Oneness isn’t turning you into me; it’s both of us belonging to God together

v: He answered, “Haven’t you read that he who made them from the beginning made them male and female,
and said, ‘For this cause a man shall leave his father and mother, and shall be joined to his wife; and the two shall become one flesh’?
So that they are no more two, but one flesh. What therefore God has joined together, don’t let man tear apart.”

lessons.still: Pause for a moment and consider: what does the word “we” mean to you? Ask the Holy Spirit to help you look at your home today through the word “we” instead of “I.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Trying to remake my spouse in my own image is another form of self on the throne; it’s me trying to take God’s place in doing his work in that person. Only the self-emptied can be one: when both are willing to be changed by Christ, both grow more like Christ, and so grow more and more one.
lessons.jesus: Jesus prayed for his disciples: “that they may all be one; even as you, Father, are in me, and I in you” (John 17:21). The Father and the Son are distinct persons, yet perfectly one. Jesus shows us that the deepest oneness doesn’t erase differences; it is each helping the other flourish in love.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for joining us together and making us one flesh. Forgive the part of us that wants to control and remake each other. Help us appreciate our differences and learn to serve each other through them, so that others may see your glory in our unity. Amen.
teach: Jesus said: “So that they are no more two, but one flesh” (Matthew 19:6). One flesh isn’t one plus one equals two; it’s one plus one equals one. It’s like mixing two paints into a new color that can never be separated back into the originals. Marriage creates a new “us.”

Yet many couples misunderstand oneness. They think it means “you have to become like me”: the same tastes, the same schedule, the same opinions. That’s actually control, not unity. True oneness is like the human body: the eye and the hand are different, yet they belong to the same body, need each other, and serve each other. Differences aren’t the enemy of oneness; they are its richness.

Jesus went on: “What therefore God has joined together, don’t let man tear apart” (Matthew 19:6). Notice that it’s God who joins us together. Oneness isn’t something we manufacture by effort; it’s a fact God has already accomplished. Our practice is to live out that fact: thinking “we” when we spend money, thinking “we” when we plan our time, and thinking “we” when we make decisions.
q: Have I ever tried to remake my spouse to be just like me? In what ways?
Which difference between us is actually God’s blessing to our home?
talk: What do you think is our biggest difference? How has that difference ever helped our home?
Was there something recently that I decided as “I” instead of “we”?
acts: Name one trait in which your spouse is different from you and that you truly appreciate
As you talk today, watch for chances to change “I” into “we”
Discuss one family decision for this week together, then decide it together
lessons.noon: “What therefore God has joined together, don’t let man tear apart” — Lord, right now I thank you for joining us together.

lessons.title: Inviting Jesus to the Wedding
lessons.theme: When a marriage runs out of wine, Jesus can turn water into wine

v: When the wine ran out, Jesus’ mother said to him, “They have no wine.”
Jesus said to her, “Woman, what does that have to do with you and me? My hour has not yet come.”
His mother said to the servants, “Whatever he says to you, do it.”
Now there were six water pots of stone set there after the Jews’ way of purifying, containing two or three metretes apiece.
Jesus said to them, “Fill the water pots with water.” So they filled them up to the brim.
He said to them, “Now draw some out, and take it to the ruler of the feast.” So they took it.
When the ruler of the feast tasted the water now become wine, and didn’t know where it came from (but the servants who had drawn the water knew), the ruler of the feast called the bridegroom
and said to him, “Everyone serves the good wine first, and when the guests have drunk freely, then that which is worse. You have kept the good wine until now!”

lessons.still: Imagine your home is the wedding feast at Cana. Quietly tell the Lord: “Lord Jesus, some things in our home have run out.” You don’t need to rush to an answer; just set your empty jars before him.
lessons.light: 321 Light: When the wine runs out, the self-ruled reaction is blame: “It’s all because you didn’t plan ahead!” The self-emptied reaction is to turn to Jesus: “Lord, we have no wine.” When our focus is on Jesus, not on ourselves, not on others, not on our circumstances, there is room for a miracle to happen.
lessons.jesus: Jesus was invited to the wedding, and he came. He didn’t decline because it was just an ordinary wedding, and he didn’t ignore the problem because it wasn’t “spiritual” enough. Jesus cares about a couple’s joy, and he is willing to step into the most ordinary and most awkward moments of our home.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, we formally invite you into our marriage. Whatever has run out, please fill it yourself; whatever you tell us, we are willing to do. Please save the best wine for the later years of our marriage, and let us experience your glory all our lives. Amen.
teach: Jesus’ first miracle didn’t happen in the temple or on a battlefield, but at a wedding. That day the wine ran out, and in that culture it would have been a lifelong embarrassment for the couple. Many marriages also have times when “the wine runs out”: the passion is spent, the patience is spent, even the things to talk about are spent.

Mary said to the servants: “Whatever he says to you, do it” (John 2:5). What Jesus told them to do was ordinary: fill the jars with water. The servants obeyed, “So they filled them up to the brim” (John 2:7). Miracles often begin with ordinary obedience. An apology today, a hug, a time of praying together: that is the water poured into the jars.

The master of the feast said: “You have kept the good wine until now!” (John 2:10). This is how Jesus works in a marriage: he can save the best for later. However long you’ve been married and however many disappointments you’ve been through, if you invite Jesus into your home and do what he says, your best days may still be ahead.
q: What in our marriage has “run out” right now?
What ordinary thing might Jesus be telling me to do as the water to pour into the jars?
talk: If Jesus sat at our dinner table tonight, what one thing would you most want to ask him to help our home with?
From this week’s lessons, which line touched you the most?
acts: Do one small act of obedience today: be the first to apologize, to hug, or to pray
Say together with your spouse: “Lord Jesus, welcome to our home.”
Write down one thing you believe God wants to do in your marriage as he “kept the good wine until now”
lessons.noon: “Whatever he says to you, do it” — Lord Jesus, right now I am willing to do what you say.

2.title: Your Spouse: God’s Gift of a Helper

mem.t: The LORD God said, “It is not good for the man to be alone. I will make him a helper comparable to him.”

date.t: Thank You for Being My Help
s: Take a walk or share a warm drink together, and each think back: over this past year, where did my spouse help me in the most practical way?
Take turns finishing this sentence: “You are God’s gift to me, because you help me...” When the speaker finishes, the listener answers only “Thank you”: no explaining, no brushing it off.
Exchange one small request: “This week, what I most need your help with is...” Each of you write down the other’s request.
Read Genesis 2:18 together, then hold hands and pray: “Lord, thank you for not leaving us alone. Make us a help to each other.”

lessons.title: “Not Good to Be Alone”
lessons.theme: God himself sees our loneliness and provides a companion

v: The LORD God said, “It is not good for the man to be alone. I will make him a helper comparable to him.”

Out of the ground the LORD God formed every animal of the field, and every bird of the sky, and brought them to the man to see what he would call them. Whatever the man called every living creature became its name.
The man gave names to all livestock, and to the birds of the sky, and to every animal of the field; but for man there was not found a helper comparable to him.

lessons.still: Be still and notice what your heart feels right now: contentment, or a touch of loneliness? You don’t need to hide it. Tell the Lord: “Lord, you see my needs, and you see our home.” Let his gaze rest on you first.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The self-ruled heart thinks it can do just fine alone, needing no one and owing no one. Admitting “I need you” is actually returning to our rightful place as creatures. Let people be people: I am a limited human being, and God uses my spouse to make up for my limits.
lessons.jesus: On his most anguished night in Gethsemane, Jesus said to his disciples: “My soul is exceedingly sorrowful, even to death. Stay here and watch with me” (Matthew 26:38). Even the Son of God did not hide his need for companions. Jesus shows us that saying “please stay with me” isn’t weakness; it’s honesty.
lessons.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for seeing human loneliness and for providing us for each other. We admit that sometimes, though we live together, our hearts are far apart. Tear down the invisible walls between us. Help us stop living alone side by side, and instead open up to each other, keep each other company, and live together in your presence. Amen.
teach: Genesis 1 reads like a poem, repeating again and again that God saw it was good. But in chapter 2, for the first time God says “not good”: “It is not good for the man to be alone. I will make him a helper comparable to him” (Genesis 2:18). There was no sin yet, the garden was perfect, and the man lived in God’s presence, yet God said something was missing. We were created to need relationship. That isn’t weakness; it is God’s original design.

Interestingly, God didn’t make the woman right away. First he brought every animal and bird to the man and let him name them one by one. When the naming was done, the text says: “but for man there was not found a helper comparable to him” (Genesis 2:20). It’s as if God first let Adam discover for himself that however rich creation was, nothing could fill that place. God often leads us this way: first he lets us see our need, then he helps us treasure his provision.

This doesn’t mean single people are incomplete; Jesus himself never married, and God also answers human loneliness through the church, friends, and family. But for those of us who are married, this verse reminds us that our spouse is God’s answer to “not good to be alone.” Sadly, many couples live under one roof while their hearts live alone: one scrolling a phone, the other watching TV, so close and yet a world apart.
q: In our marriage, when do I feel that we live “under one roof while our hearts live alone”?
Do I often refuse to admit that I need my spouse? What lies behind that?
talk: Was there a moment recently when you felt lonely but didn’t say anything? I’d like to hear about it.
What time of day works best for us to put our phones down and really be together for ten minutes?
acts: Say to your spouse today: “With you here, I’m not alone.”
Put your phones in another room during a meal
Before bed, spend five minutes asking your spouse about the happiest and the most tiring parts of their day
lessons.noon: “It is not good for the man to be alone. I will make him a helper comparable to him” — Lord, thank you for not leaving me alone. Right now I give thanks for my spouse.

lessons.title: Helper: A Name God Uses for Himself
lessons.theme: “Helper” is not second-class; it’s one of God’s own titles

v: I will lift up my eyes to the hills. Where does my help come from?
My help comes from the LORD, who made heaven and earth.
Our soul has waited for the LORD. He is our help and our shield.

lessons.still: Lift your head and imagine yourself, like the psalmist, lifting your eyes to the hills. Say softly: “My help comes from the LORD, who made heaven and earth.” Let these words sink slowly into your heart, and hand him the thing you most need help with today.
lessons.light: 321 Light: A proud heart feels that helping others is beneath it and always wants to be the star. But God himself was willing to be a helper, and that is the glory of humility. When we stop keeping score of who’s more important, humility draws out humility, and husband and wife become each other’s strength.
lessons.jesus: Jesus said: “For the Son of Man also came not to be served but to serve” (Mark 10:45). The Lord of the universe came to earth and chose to be a helper: healing the sick, feeding the hungry, lifting up the weak. Jesus shows us that the greatest is the one most willing to help.
lessons.pray: God our helper, thank you for being our help at all times. We admit that we often want to be served but don’t want to serve; we want to be the star but don’t want to step in where we’re needed. Make us more like you, reaching out where the other is weak and becoming each other’s strength, and let this home stand firm through your help. Amen.
teach: When people hear the word “helper,” many picture an assistant, an errand-runner, a sidekick, as if someone else is the star and we’re just the supporting cast. But the word for “helper” in Genesis 2:18 is the Hebrew ezer, and in the Old Testament it is used most often to describe God himself. The psalmist says: “My help comes from the LORD, who made heaven and earth” (Psalm 121:2).

Another psalm says: “He is our help and our shield” (Psalm 33:20). Moses named his son Eliezer, meaning “my God is help,” because “My father’s God was my help” (Exodus 18:4). God helped Israel not because he was beneath Israel, but because he had strength and love and was willing to reach out. So “helper” isn’t about rank; it’s a love that has power: filling in, with what you have, the places where the other falls short.

In Genesis 2:18 the helper is “comparable to him”; the Hebrew carries the sense of “corresponding to him, facing him, matching him,” like two puzzle pieces fitting together face to face. The wife God made is not her husband’s accessory but a companion equal to him in dignity and suited to him. Going further, God’s heart is for both husband and wife to learn this ezer kind of love: to become the other’s strength when they are weak.
q: When I hear the word “helper,” is my first reaction a sense of honor, or of being slighted? Why?
In what area do I really need my spouse’s help but feel awkward asking?
talk: In our home, where do you think you most often become my ezer, my helper? I want to thank you.
Is there something recently where you wish I would help a bit more? Just name one specific thing.
acts: Take the initiative today and do one task your spouse usually handles
Ask your spouse for help with one thing you need
Copy Psalm 121:2 onto a sticky note and put it by your front door
lessons.noon: “My help comes from the LORD, who made heaven and earth” — Lord, you are my help. Make me a help to my spouse as well.

lessons.title: A Gift, Not a Tool
lessons.theme: Your spouse is a gift God brought with his own hands, not a tool to satisfy you

v: The LORD God caused the man to fall into a deep sleep. As the man slept, he took one of his ribs, and closed up the flesh in its place.
The LORD God made a woman from the rib which he had taken from the man, and brought her to the man.
The man said, “This is now bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh. She will be called ‘woman,’ because she was taken out of Man.”
House and riches are an inheritance from fathers, but a prudent wife is from the LORD.

lessons.still: Imagine someone holding a wrapped gift in both hands, walking right up to you. Quietly tell the Lord: “Lord, thank you for bringing him/her to me.” Let gratitude come before every demand.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Treating your spouse as a tool is how the self-ruled life sees: everything centers on my needs. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. When we stop asking “What can you do for me?” and start giving thanks that “God gave you to me,” marriage moves from a transaction back to grace.
lessons.jesus: When Jesus prayed for his disciples, he said: “I revealed your name to the people whom you have given me out of the world” (John 17:6). The disciples were often weak, argued over who was greatest, and failed to understand, yet Jesus always saw them as gifts from the Father and gave himself fully to keeping them. Jesus teaches us to see the people around us this way.
lessons.pray: Father, giver of every good gift, thank you for bringing us to each other with your own hands. We admit that we often see only where the other falls short, and treat each other as tools for our own satisfaction. Open our eyes to see each other again as gifts from you; let gratitude replace fault-finding and cherishing replace demanding. Amen.
teach: What’s the biggest difference between a tool and a gift? A tool’s value lies in how well it works; when it breaks, you replace it. A gift’s value lies in who gave it; however old it gets, you can’t bear to throw it away. Much of the disappointment in marriage comes from quietly treating our spouse as a tool: satisfied when they earn money, take care of the home, and meet our needs, but quick to complain once they stop “working well.”

Genesis says that God made the woman and “brought her to the man” (Genesis 2:22). This was the Bible’s first wedding: God himself walked the bride over and gave her to the groom. When Adam saw her, the first words the Bible records him saying were a poem of wonder: “This is now bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh” (Genesis 2:23). What he saw wasn’t a tool, but a gift God had brought with his own hands.

Proverbs also says: “House and riches are an inheritance from fathers, but a prudent wife is from the LORD” (Proverbs 19:14). A house and wealth can be inherited from our ancestors, but a partner to walk with for life is a gift of God’s grace. This principle holds for husbands and wives alike. When we remember that our spouse is God’s gift, we will treasure the gift with the same heart that treasures the Giver, even when the wrapping shows the marks of the years.
q: How much of my recent frustration with my spouse comes from his/her not meeting my needs?
If I truly believed my spouse is a gift God brought with his own hands, how would my attitude toward him/her be different today?
talk: Do you remember what you most admired about me when we first met? Can you still see it now?
When do you feel I treat you as a “tool” instead of a “gift”? Please say it gently; I’m willing to listen.
acts: Write down three qualities in your spouse that you’re grateful for, about who they are rather than what they do for you
Say today: “Thank God for giving you to me.”
Hold back one complaint you were about to make
lessons.noon: “a prudent wife is from the LORD” — Lord, thank you for giving me my spouse. Teach me to treasure this gift.

lessons.title: Seeing Your Spouse with New Eyes
lessons.theme: Trading a human point of view for God’s, to see our spouse as God sees him or her

v: But the LORD said to Samuel, “Don’t look on his face, or on the height of his stature, because I have rejected him; for I don’t see as man sees. For man looks at the outward appearance, but the LORD looks at the heart.”
Therefore we know no one according to the flesh from now on. Even though we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him so no more.
Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new.

lessons.still: Close your eyes and picture your spouse’s face. Don’t think about his/her faults for now. Simply and quietly ask: “Lord, lend me your eyes, so I can see him/her as you see him/her.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: From the human point of view to God’s, from earth to heaven. If our focus is on our spouse’s faults, the more we look the more weary we grow; if our focus is on Jesus, we can see him at work in our spouse. Change your mindset and your life will change: put on new eyes, and the relationship will change too.
lessons.jesus: The first time Simon came to Jesus, Jesus looked at him and said: “You are Simon the son of Jonah. You shall be called Cephas” (John 1:42). At that point Peter was impulsive and unsteady, yet Jesus called him “Rock.” When Jesus looks at people, he sees who God is going to make them.
lessons.pray: Lord, heal our nearsighted eyes. We so often look at each other by outward appearance and by performance, and what we see is mostly faults. Give us your eyes, to see each other as people you love and are shaping, patient with the present and hopeful for the future. Amen.
teach: When a nearsighted person puts on the right glasses, the world suddenly comes into focus: every leaf on the tree by the road is different. After years of marriage, we easily become “nearsighted” toward our spouse: we see only his socks left lying around, her repeated reminders, each other’s old habits, but we can’t see God’s purposes in the other person. We need a new pair of glasses.

When Samuel went to anoint a new king, he too was drawn by outward looks. God told him: “man looks at the outward appearance, but the LORD looks at the heart” (1 Samuel 16:7). Paul also says: “we know no one according to the flesh from now on” (2 Corinthians 5:16). To know someone “according to the flesh” means to use worldly standards: their qualifications, their performance, whether they meet my needs.

What is God’s point of view? “Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation” (2 Corinthians 5:17). If your spouse is a believer, he/she is a new creation God is still sculpting: not finished yet, but with a sure outcome. If your spouse doesn’t yet believe, he/she is still someone God loves and is seeking. When we see with God’s eyes, we can be patient with who our spouse is now and hopeful about who they will become.
q: Lately, which “glasses” have I most often worn when I look at my spouse: criticism, comparison, disappointment, or hope?
If Jesus gave my spouse a new name, what might he call him/her?
talk: I want to tell you one thing I see God doing in you: ... (take turns finishing this sentence)
In what area do you wish I would look at you with hope rather than disappointment? If your spouse can’t join you for now, write down what you’d like to say to them.
acts: Say at least once today: “I’ve seen you grow in...”
When you feel like criticizing your spouse, first pray one sentence for him/her in your heart
Write down a “new name in God’s eyes” for your spouse
lessons.noon: “man looks at the outward appearance, but the LORD looks at the heart” — Lord, right now lend me your eyes to see my spouse’s heart.

lessons.title: I Want to Be Your Help
lessons.theme: From expecting my spouse to help me, to becoming my spouse’s help first

v: Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ.
Therefore exhort one another, and build each other up, even as you also do.

lessons.still: Look back over this week: God showed you that it’s not good to be alone, showed you the dignity of the helper, showed you that your spouse is a gift. Now quietly ask the Lord: “Lord, how can I be his/her help today?”
lessons.light: 321 Light: In a self-ruled marriage, both partners wait for the other to change first and give first; in a self-emptied marriage, both race to be the first to lift the other up. Change begins with me. I become the helper first, not because my spouse deserves it, but because Jesus treated me this way first.
lessons.jesus: After washing his disciples’ feet, Jesus said: “For I have given you an example, that you should also do as I have done to you” (John 13:15). He knew he was about to suffer; his burden was heavier than anyone’s. Yet he still bent down and saw his disciples’ needs first. This is the model of a helper.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for bending down to wash our feet and carrying our heaviest burden. Help us stop simply waiting to be helped and instead become each other’s help first: noticing the other’s weariness, speaking words that hold each other up, and reaching out a helping hand. May our home be a place you see as good. Amen.
teach: Picture two people carrying a heavy table together. If each only lifts their own end and complains that the other isn’t lifting high enough, the table soon tilts. If each pays attention to whether the other is straining and adjusts as needed, the table stays level. This week we’ve learned that our spouse is God’s gift of a helper; today we turn that truth around and ask: am I a helper to my spouse?

Paul says: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ” (Galatians 6:2). A burden is pressure too heavy for one person to carry: work, children, parents, illness, emotions. At home it’s easy to see only our own burden and feel “I’m tired enough already.” Bearing one another’s burdens means that even when I’m tired, I’m still willing to notice that you’re tired too.

Paul also tells us to “exhort one another, and build each other up” (1 Thessalonians 5:11). Helping isn’t only doing chores and dividing up tasks; it also means using our words to lift each other’s hearts. A simple “You’ve worked so hard” or “I’m here with you” often has more power than solving the problem. When both husband and wife turn from “You need to help me” to “Let me help you,” the home becomes the place God called “good” in his design.
q: This week, what is the biggest new insight God has given me about being a “helper”?
What is the heaviest burden on my spouse’s shoulders right now? Do I really know?
talk: What’s the heaviest burden on your shoulders lately? What part of it could I carry with you?
From this week’s lessons, which line touched you the most? What does it make you want to say to me?
acts: Ask your spouse: “Is there anything I can do for you today?” Then do it
Say to your spouse: “You’ve worked so hard. I’m here with you.”
Pray specifically, once, about the heaviest burden your spouse is carrying
lessons.noon: “Bear one another’s burdens” — Lord, right now let me see my spouse’s burden and carry it with him/her.

3.title: A Covenant, Not a Contract: What God Has Joined

mem.t: So that they are no more two, but one flesh. What therefore God has joined together, don’t let man tear apart.”

s: Look together at your wedding rings (or your marriage certificate or wedding photos), and each share: when you said “I do,” what was going through your mind?
Take turns sharing one time when “we might have given up, but we didn’t,” and tell how God kept you through it.
Write together a covenant statement of your own, for example: “In good times and bad, we choose each other, and we choose Jesus.”
Hold hands and read Matthew 19:6, then pray: “Lord, you joined us together. Be the witness and the keeper of our covenant.”

lessons.title: Contract and Covenant
lessons.theme: A contract is about conditions; a covenant is about commitment

v: He said to him, “Bring me a heifer three years old, a female goat three years old, a ram three years old, a turtledove, and a young pigeon.”
He brought him all these, and divided them in the middle, and laid each half opposite the other; but he didn’t divide the birds.
It came to pass that, when the sun went down, and it was dark, behold, a smoking furnace and a flaming torch passed between these pieces.
In that day the LORD made a covenant with Abram, saying, “I have given this land to your offspring, from the river of Egypt to the great river, the river Euphrates:

lessons.still: Be still and consider: in our marriage, am I hiding some “I’ll do it only if you...” in my heart? You don’t need to rush to change it; just lay it honestly before the Lord.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The contract mindset is centered on me, always calculating gains and losses and protecting myself; that is exactly the self-ruled life. The covenant mindset puts the focus on God and on my spouse, asking first “How can I keep the covenant?” rather than “Have you kept it?” Change your mindset and your life will change.
lessons.jesus: At the Last Supper, Jesus took the cup and said: “This cup is the new covenant in my blood, which is poured out for you” (Luke 22:20). His disciples were about to run away and deny him, yet Jesus still made a covenant with his own life. Jesus’ love is not a contract; it is a covenant guaranteed with his blood.
lessons.pray: Covenant-keeping God of steadfast love, thank you for walking alone between those pieces, and for making a new covenant with us through the blood of Jesus. We admit that we often calculate gains and losses with a contract heart. Renew us, so that our marriage is built not on conditions but on your faithfulness, and we stay committed to each other for life. Amen.
teach: When you rent a home you sign a contract: the landlord provides the house, the tenant pays rent on time, and if either side breaks the terms, the contract can be ended. At the heart of a contract is the word “if”: if you do your part, I’ll do mine. Without realizing it, many people run their marriage with a contract mindset: “I’ll be good to you if you’re good to me; if you won’t change, I don’t have to either.” But the marriage God established is not a contract. It is a covenant.

Genesis 15 records an ancient covenant ceremony. The animals were cut in two, and Abram “laid each half opposite the other” (Genesis 15:10). By the custom of the day, both parties would walk between the pieces, as if to say: “If I break this covenant, may I become like these animals.” It was a commitment guaranteed with one’s life. In fact, the Hebrew expression for making a covenant literally means “to cut a covenant.”

The amazing thing is that on that day only “a smoking furnace and a flaming torch passed between these pieces” (Genesis 15:17), the sign of God’s presence, while Abram lay in a deep sleep. God walked through alone, as if to say: “The cost of keeping this covenant, I will bear by myself.” At the heart of a covenant is not “if” but “I will”: whatever you are like, I commit myself to you. This is how God treats us, and it is the foundation of marriage.
q: Which of the things I do for my spouse actually come with the condition “You be good to me first, then I’ll be good to you”?
In what situations do I most often “keep score” in my heart of who gives more in our marriage?
talk: Where in our marriage do you think things look more like a “contract” and need to turn back into a “covenant” together?
Was there a time when you felt me standing by you unconditionally? How did that feel?
acts: Today, do one thing to love your spouse without expecting anything in return
When you notice yourself thinking “I’ll do it only if you...,” change it to “I will...”
Write “A covenant, not a contract” in the notes app on your phone
lessons.noon: “This cup is the new covenant in my blood, which is poured out for you” — Lord Jesus, thank you for making a covenant with me with your life. Teach me to love like this too.

lessons.title: God Stands Between Us as Witness
lessons.theme: The marriage covenant is made before God; God honors the covenant and protects the oppressed

v: Yet you say, ‘Why?’ Because the LORD has been witness between you and the wife of your youth, against whom you have dealt treacherously, though she is your companion and the wife of your covenant.

Did he not make you one, although he had the residue of the Spirit? Why one? He sought godly offspring. Therefore take heed to your spirit, and let no one deal treacherously against the wife of his youth.
One who hates and divorces”, says the LORD, the God of Israel, “covers his garment with violence!” says the LORD of Armies. “Therefore pay attention to your spirit, that you don’t be unfaithful.

lessons.still: Imagine God sitting right between the two of you, looking at you with both tenderness and justice. Quietly tell him: “Lord, you are the witness of our marriage covenant. I want to be honest before you.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Dealing treacherously is what the self-ruled heart does for its own convenience, sacrificing the other person in the covenant. To let God be God is to acknowledge that my marriage has a witness; to let people be people is to treat my spouse with honesty, respect, and protection, never oppressing and never hiding.
lessons.jesus: Jesus said: “let your ‘Yes’ be ‘Yes’ and your ‘No’ be ‘No’” (Matthew 5:37). His whole life, his words matched his actions; he never covered one way of living with nice-sounding words. Jesus shows us that for someone who lives before God, a promise is a promise, with no need for extra oaths to prove it.
lessons.pray: God of justice and love, thank you for being the witness of our marriage covenant and for watching over everyone who is wronged and oppressed. Guard our hearts so that we never treat each other with treachery or violence; make our home the safest place for each other. And protect every family that is in danger right now; open a way out for them. Amen.
teach: In Malachi’s day, the people wept at the altar and couldn’t understand why God no longer accepted their offerings. The prophet answered: “Because the LORD has been witness between you and the wife of your youth” (Malachi 2:14). In those days many husbands casually divorced the wives they had married when young. God was saying: how you treat your spouse directly affects your relationship with me.

God calls her “your companion and the wife of your covenant” (Malachi 2:14). The marriage covenant isn’t a private agreement between two people; it is a covenant made before God, and he is the witness. Just as a notary is present when a contract is signed, God himself witnesses a marriage. So the prophet warns twice: “take heed to your spirit” (Malachi 2:15). Keeping covenant doesn’t begin with big things; it begins with guarding the small thoughts of the heart.

Verse 16 is translated in different ways, but its message is clear. The WEB puts it this way: “One who hates and divorces... covers his garment with violence!” (Malachi 2:16). God hates covenant-breaking, and he hates violence just as much. So let it be said plainly: physical, verbal, sexual, and financial abuse and control are in themselves a breaking of the covenant, and God does not want anyone to stay in danger and endure it. If you are in a situation like this, your safety comes first. Please seek help from a pastor and from professionals as soon as possible.
q: If God were sitting right between us, which of my recent words or attitudes would make me feel ashamed?
Are there small thoughts in my heart slowly wearing down my commitment to our marriage covenant?
talk: When you think of “God standing between us as witness,” what comforts you most?
In our home, what kinds of words or actions make you feel most safe? If your spouse can’t join you for now, write down the kind of safety you hope to create for him or her.
acts: Pay attention to your tone of voice today, and use no mocking or threatening words
Tell your spouse: “I remember what I said before God.”
If someone you know is in a dangerous marriage, pray for them and go with them to seek help
lessons.noon: “Therefore take heed to your spirit” — Lord, right now guard my heart, so that I keep covenant honestly before you.

lessons.title: The Weight of a Vow
lessons.theme: “I do” is a promise we spend a lifetime keeping

v: When you vow a vow to God, don’t defer to pay it; for he has no pleasure in fools. Pay that which you vow.
It is better that you should not vow, than that you should vow and not pay.
in whose eyes a vile man is despised, but who honors those who fear the LORD; he who keeps an oath even when it hurts, and doesn’t change;

lessons.still: Recall the “I do” you spoke at your wedding. However moved or nervous you were when you said it, gently bring it before the Lord: “Lord, today I want to hear again how much these words weigh.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: The self-ruled heart keeps its vows by asking whether it’s worth it for me; the self-emptied heart keeps its vows by asking whether God receives the glory. Our vows aren’t our achievement; they are a response of faith. We say “I do” because we trust the God who makes us able.
lessons.jesus: In the garden of Gethsemane, Jesus prayed: “not my will, but yours, be done” (Luke 22:42). He knew the cross lay ahead and the cost was enormous, yet he did not take back his commitment. Jesus shows us that a true “I will” is saying “I will” even at the hardest moment.
lessons.pray: Lord, we once said “I do” before you. Thank you for always remembering those words and for always helping us keep them. In good times, keep us from taking them lightly; in hard times, keep us from giving up. By your grace, may every promise we have spoken become true. Amen.
teach: Wedding vows are usually only a few lines: “For better, for worse, for richer, for poorer, in sickness and in health, to love and to cherish, till death do us part.” Saying them takes less than a minute, but keeping them takes a lifetime. It’s like signing a blank check: you don’t know what amount will be filled in later, but the moment you sign, you’ve already agreed.

The Teacher says: “When you vow a vow to God, don’t defer to pay it” (Ecclesiastes 5:4), and again: “It is better that you should not vow, than that you should vow and not pay” (Ecclesiastes 5:5). In the Bible a vow is serious business, because it is spoken to God. Wedding vows aren’t spoken only to our spouse; they are spoken before God. When we’re tempted to cut corners on them, we should remember that it wasn’t only our spouse who heard those words. God heard them too.

The psalm describes the one who may live on God’s holy hill: “he who keeps an oath even when it hurts, and doesn’t change” (Psalm 15:4). The worth of a vow shows most clearly when keeping it hurts. Keeping covenant in good times isn’t hard; keeping it in hard times reveals how much a vow weighs. Of course, keeping covenant isn’t a matter of gritting our teeth and toughing it out. It means returning to God every day and asking for his strength, so that the words we spoke become true one day at a time.
q: Which line of our wedding vows is hardest for me to keep right now?
Has there been a recent moment when keeping my word cost me, and I wanted to take back my commitment?
talk: Do you remember any lines from our vows? Try recalling them together, and share which line means the most to you.
Of the hard times we’ve been through, when do you think we most clearly kept the vows we made back then?
acts: Find your wedding vows (or recall the gist of them) and read them through today
Choose one line of your vows and live it out in a concrete way today
Today, follow through on one small thing you promised your spouse
lessons.noon: “he who keeps an oath even when it hurts, and doesn’t change” — Lord, right now make the “I do” I once spoke still count today.

lessons.title: Not Giving Up Easily
lessons.theme: We can hold on because God never gives up on us

v: But I will not completely take my loving kindness from him, nor allow my faithfulness to fail.
I will not break my covenant, nor alter what my lips have uttered.
If we are faithless, he remains faithful; for he can’t deny himself.”

lessons.still: If you feel weary right now, even a little like giving up, don’t blame yourself. Just hand this weariness to the Lord and tell him: “Lord, I’m tired, but I know you have never given up on me.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: The urge to give up often comes from a misplaced focus: looking only at my spouse’s failures, my own grievances, and my present circumstances. When our focus is on Jesus, we look past the temporary to the eternal. God is still at work and the story isn’t finished yet, so we have reason to hold on one more day and love one more time.
lessons.jesus: As Jesus was about to leave his disciples, he promised: “I will not leave you orphans. I will come to you” (John 14:18). His disciples were about to fail and scatter, yet Jesus did not take back his promise. He never gives up on the weak, and that gives us courage to keep holding on in our marriage.
lessons.pray: Faithful God, thank you for never withdrawing your loving kindness and never breaking your covenant. When we are weary, disappointed, and ready to give up, hold us up yourself, so that we choose each other once again. And protect all who are in danger; bring them safety and help. Amen.
teach: When a child learns to ride a bike, the parent holds the bike from behind. If the child falls, the parent doesn’t say, “You’re hopeless, give up.” They pick the child up and try again. God treats his people the same way. In Psalm 89, God says that even if David’s descendants forsake his law, he will discipline them, “But I will not completely take my loving kindness from him, nor allow my faithfulness to fail” (Psalm 89:33).

God goes on: “I will not break my covenant, nor alter what my lips have uttered” (Psalm 89:34). Paul also says: “If we are faithless, he remains faithful; for he can’t deny himself” (2 Timothy 2:13). We can hold on in marriage not because we’re especially strong, but because the God we trust is a God who doesn’t give up. The way he treats us becomes our model for how we treat our spouse.

Not giving up easily means that in seasons of disappointment, conflict, and coldness, we don’t make “leaving” our first option, but go back to God together and seek restoration. But this does not mean staying in danger. If there is violence, threats, or control in a marriage, protecting your own safety and your children’s is the responsible choice. Forgiveness and reconciliation also have to happen on the basis of safety, step by step, with pastors and professionals walking alongside.
q: Has the thought “Forget it” crossed my mind lately? About what?
When I recall how God has never given up on me, how does that change the way I see my spouse?
talk: What was the hardest season of our marriage? What brought us through it?
When you’re exhausted and disappointed, how do you most want me to be with you? If your spouse can’t join you for now, write down the encouragement you’d like to give him or her.
acts: Say to your spouse: “Let’s keep going together.”
Write down a time when God didn’t give up on you
If your marriage is struggling, reach out to a pastor you trust this week
lessons.noon: “If we are faithless, he remains faithful” — Faithful Lord, right now thank you for never giving up on me. Help me not to give up either.

lessons.title: A Covenant Written on the Heart
lessons.theme: The power to keep covenant comes not from willpower but from the new heart God gives

v: “Behold, the days come,” says the LORD, “that I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel, and with the house of Judah,

not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers in the day that I took them by the hand to bring them out of the land of Egypt, which covenant of mine they broke, although I was a husband to them,” says the LORD.

“But this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days,” says the LORD: “I will put my law in their inward parts, and I will write it in their heart. I will be their God, and they shall be my people.

lessons.still: This week we’ve seen the weight of covenant, and perhaps we’ve also seen our own weakness. Be still, put your hand on your heart, and tell the Lord: “Lord, I can’t keep this on my own. Please write your covenant on my heart.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Keeping covenant in my own strength is another form of self on the throne: thinking that if I just try hard enough, I can do it. Being self-emptied means admitting I can’t, and letting Christ live in me. It isn’t that I kept the covenant; it’s that the covenant-keeping God kept us.
lessons.jesus: Scripture says: “having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end” (John 13:1). Jesus knew Judas would betray him and Peter would deny him, yet he loved them to the end. His love isn’t an occasional feeling; it’s a commitment that lasts to the end. This is the love he wants to place in our hearts through the Holy Spirit.
lessons.pray: God of the new covenant, thank you for not giving up on us when we broke covenant, but instead writing your covenant on our hearts through the blood of Jesus. We admit that we can’t keep this covenant on our own. Holy Spirit, renew us every day, so that love grows from within us and we walk with you and with each other all our lives. Amen.
teach: Many people make New Year’s resolutions to exercise or go to bed early, then give up within a few weeks. Willpower alone rarely lasts. The marriage covenant is the same. This week we’ve learned about covenant, vows, and not giving up, but if we just listen and then grit our teeth to do it, we’ll soon wear out. What we need isn’t just more determination, but a new heart.

Through Jeremiah, God said that Israel had broken the covenant: “which covenant of mine they broke, although I was a husband to them” (Jeremiah 31:32). God didn’t give up there; instead he promised a new covenant: “I will put my law in their inward parts, and I will write it in their heart” (Jeremiah 31:33). The old covenant was carved on tablets of stone, making demands from the outside; the new covenant is written on the heart, changing us from the inside.

This is the gospel: Jesus’ death dealt with the sin of our covenant-breaking, Jesus’ resurrection gives us new life, and the Holy Spirit lives in us, making us willing and able to keep covenant. Jesus said: “What therefore God has joined together, don’t let man tear apart” (Matthew 19:6). It is God who joined us together, and it is God who gives us strength from within to live out this covenant day by day.
q: This week, what have I relied on most to keep my commitment to our marriage: willpower, a sense of duty, or God’s grace?
Which place in my heart most needs God to write his will on it again?
talk: Of this week’s lessons on covenant, which idea most changed how you see our marriage?
If we wrote a “covenant statement” for our home, what words would you want in it?
acts: Tell God today: “Lord, I can’t, but you can.”
Write your covenant statement together with your spouse
Recite Matthew 19:6 from memory to your spouse
lessons.noon: “I will put my law in their inward parts, and I will write it in their heart” — Lord, right now write your love on my heart, so that I can keep covenant.

4.title: A Great Mystery: Christ and the Church

mem.t: This mystery is great, but I speak concerning Christ and the assembly.

s: Go together to a place with a far view (a hilltop, the beach, a tall building, or a park), or simply stand at a window at home, and spend five quiet minutes enjoying what God has made.
Take turns sharing: what in our marriage has shown you the love of Jesus?
Imagine yourselves twenty years from now, and each finish this sentence: “By then, I hope people will see in us...”
Read Ephesians 5:32 together and pray: “Lord, may our marriage be a picture of your love for the church.”

lessons.title: Marriage Is a Picture
lessons.theme: Earthly marriage is a shadow that points to Christ and the church

v: For no man ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it, even as the Lord also does the assembly,
because we are members of his body, of his flesh and bones.
“For this cause a man will leave his father and mother and will be joined to his wife. Then the two will become one flesh.”
This mystery is great, but I speak concerning Christ and the assembly.

lessons.still: Be still and think of the photo your family treasures most. Then tell the Lord: “Lord, let our marriage also be a photo that helps people see you.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Thinking marriage exists just to meet my needs is seeing it from the human point of view; seeing that marriage exists to display Christ is seeing it from God’s point of view. When our focus turns from ourselves to Jesus, marriage moves from our small “us” into God’s eternal purpose.
lessons.jesus: Jesus said: “The Kingdom of Heaven is like a certain king, who made a wedding feast for his son” (Matthew 22:2). He often used wedding feasts to explain the kingdom, because marriage best expresses the joy, intimacy, and commitment between God and his people. Jesus shows us that every wedding is a preview of a far greater wedding.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for revealing this great mystery, showing us that marriage speaks of you and the church. Our picture isn’t perfect; please restore it yourself. Help us nourish and cherish each other, so that people catch a glimpse in our home of how you love the church. Amen.
teach: However beautiful your vacation photos are, they aren’t the scenery itself; yet a good photo can make someone who’s never been there want to go and see for themselves. Paul says earthly marriage is a photo like that. After quoting Genesis 2:24, he goes on: “This mystery is great, but I speak concerning Christ and the assembly” (Ephesians 5:32), that is, the church. When God established marriage, he already had another marriage in mind.

In the Bible, a “mystery” isn’t something strange and hard to understand; it’s something once hidden and now revealed. People used to think marriage was simply a man and a woman uniting and starting a family. Now, through the gospel, we see clearly that God established marriage as a picture anyone can understand, portraying how Christ loves the church. Paul says that a man “nourishes and cherishes” his own body, “even as the Lord also does the assembly” (Ephesians 5:29), “because we are members of his body” (Ephesians 5:30).

This changes how we see marriage. Our marriage isn’t just “the two of us”; it’s a picture God has hung up in the world. The picture may be stained or torn, but its subject hasn’t changed: Christ loves the church. So whenever we nourish and cherish each other, we add a brushstroke to the picture, helping people catch a glimpse of the far more beautiful Bridegroom.
q: What did I used to think was the main purpose of marriage? How is that different from what Paul says?
If people could only come to know Christ through our marriage, what kind of Christ would they see?
talk: In the picture that is our marriage, which brushstroke do you think best shows people the love of Jesus?
In what way do I “nourish and cherish” you that you feel most? Where would you like a little more?
acts: Today, “nourish and cherish” your spouse with one concrete action, like bringing a glass of water or rubbing their shoulders
Memorize Ephesians 5:32
Choose a photo of the two of you and write on the back: “May people see Christ in us.”
lessons.noon: “This mystery is great, but I speak concerning Christ and the assembly” — Lord, right now may our marriage be a picture that points to you.

lessons.title: God, the Bridegroom Who Pursues His Bride
lessons.theme: The whole Bible tells of a Bridegroom pursuing the bride he loves

v: I will betroth you to me forever. Yes, I will betroth you to me in righteousness, in justice, in loving kindness, and in compassion.
I will even betroth you to me in faithfulness; and you shall know the LORD.
For as a young man marries a virgin, so your sons will marry you. As a bridegroom rejoices over his bride, so your God will rejoice over you.

lessons.still: Close your eyes and hear God say to you: “I will betroth you to me forever” (Hosea 2:19). However unlovable you feel today, let these words reach you first; then, with a heart that knows it is loved, go and love your spouse.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Behind many demands in marriage lies the emptiness of “I’m not loved enough.” The self-ruled heart tries to fill that emptiness from its spouse, and both end up exhausted. When we are first filled with God’s love, we stop taking from our spouse and can give out of the overflow.
lessons.jesus: When people asked why Jesus’ disciples didn’t fast, Jesus answered: “Can the groomsmen fast while the bridegroom is with them?” (Mark 2:19). Jesus called himself the bridegroom. He came to bring his bride home, and his presence brings the joy of a wedding feast.
lessons.pray: Lord, you are the Bridegroom who pursues us, winning us back with righteousness, justice, loving kindness, compassion, and faithfulness. Thank you for rejoicing over us as a bridegroom rejoices over his bride. Fill us with your love, so that we stop taking from each other and love each other out of your abundance. Amen.
teach: Some have said the Bible is a great love story: it begins with a wedding in Eden and ends with the wedding feast of the Lamb. In the Old Testament, God often describes his relationship with his people as that of a husband and a bridegroom. Even when Israel left him again and again, God still said through the prophet Hosea: “I will betroth you to me forever” (Hosea 2:19).

In ancient times, the bridegroom paid a bride-price at the betrothal. What bride-price did God pay to win his people? “I will betroth you to me in righteousness, in justice, in loving kindness, and in compassion” (Hosea 2:19), and “I will even betroth you to me in faithfulness” (Hosea 2:20). These are all God’s own attributes. God doesn’t wait for his bride to become worthy of him first; he gives everything he has to win back those who are unworthy.

Isaiah says: “As a bridegroom rejoices over his bride, so your God will rejoice over you” (Isaiah 62:5). Picture the look in a groom’s eyes as his bride walks in at the wedding; that is the delight with which God looks at us. We can love our spouse well because we have first been loved like this. Only those who are loved have the strength to love.
q: Do I truly believe that God looks at me with the delight of a bridegroom looking at his bride? What makes that hard for me to believe?
Which of my recent demands on my spouse are really attempts to get from him/her a love only God can give?
talk: Do you remember something I did while we were dating that made you feel “pursued”?
In our life now, how could I help you feel cherished and pursued again?
acts: Today, give your spouse a small surprise, just like when you were dating
Say to yourself three times in your heart: “God delights in me.”
Write your spouse a card naming one thing you treasure about him/her
lessons.noon: “As a bridegroom rejoices over his bride, so your God will rejoice over you” — Lord, right now, resting in your delight, let me delight in my spouse too.

lessons.title: Not Just Happiness, but Holiness
lessons.theme: God uses marriage to shape us into the likeness of Christ

v: We know that all things work together for good for those who love God, for those who are called according to his purpose.
For whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brothers.

lessons.still: Think of the thing in your marriage that has made you most uncomfortable lately. Don’t rush to work out who’s right and who’s wrong; simply ask the Lord: “Lord, what do you want to do in me through this?”
lessons.light: 321 Light: The self-ruled heart only wants to change its spouse so that it can be comfortable; the self-emptied heart lets God change it through its spouse. Friction in marriage isn’t necessarily a sign that the marriage is failing. It may be God wearing away our “self” so that the likeness of Christ can show through.
lessons.jesus: Jesus prayed for his disciples: “For their sakes I sanctify myself, that they themselves also may be sanctified in truth” (John 17:19). Jesus first gave himself wholly to the Father so that his disciples could be made holy too. In marriage, we don’t start by demanding that our spouse become holy; we start by offering ourselves, becoming a help to our spouse’s growth in holiness.
lessons.pray: Holy God, thank you for wanting not only our happiness but for us to become like your Son. We admit that we often want only to change each other, and are unwilling to be changed by you. Use every adjustment in our marriage to wear away our pride and self-will, so that the likeness of Christ grows clearer and clearer in us. Amen.
teach: A rough stone in a river is washed by the current day after day, knocking against other stones, until at last it becomes a smooth, round pebble. Marriage is like that river. Many people marry to find happiness. There’s nothing wrong with that; God is glad for us to have joy. But God established marriage for a deeper purpose as well: to make us holy.

Paul says: “all things work together for good for those who love God” (Romans 8:28). What is this “good”? The next verse explains: “For whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son” (Romans 8:29). The greatest good isn’t everything going smoothly; it’s becoming more and more like Christ. The adjustments, the waiting, the misunderstandings, and the reconciliations of marriage can all become tools God uses to shape us.

Paul also describes Christ giving himself up for the church “that he might sanctify her” (Ephesians 5:26), so that in the end she would be “holy and without defect” (Ephesians 5:27). This is Christ’s heart for the church, and it is the direction of marriage too. When we ask, “Is this marriage making me happy?” we can also ask, “Is this marriage making me more like Jesus?”
q: Which recent friction in our marriage might be God’s opportunity to wear down one of my rough edges?
Do I often treat “happiness” as the only measure of our marriage?
talk: Since we married, in what way do you think I’ve become more like Jesus? (Please name one specific thing.)
What kind of friction comes up between us most often? How can we hand it over to God together for him to use?
acts: Write down one rough edge in your character that you’re willing to let God change through your marriage
When friction comes up today, first ask in your heart: “Lord, what do you want to change in me?”
Tell your spouse one virtue you’ve learned from him/her
lessons.noon: “all things work together for good for those who love God” — Lord, right now I trust that you are using our marriage to make me more like Jesus.

lessons.title: Letting People Read Christ in Our Home
lessons.theme: Our marriage is a letter from Christ, read by everyone

v: You are our letter, written in our hearts, known and read by all men,
being revealed that you are a letter of Christ, served by us, written not with ink, but with the Spirit of the living God; not in tablets of stone, but in tablets that are hearts of flesh.

lessons.still: Imagine a letter lying open on your dining table, and written in it is how the two of you lived this week. Quietly ask the Lord: “Lord, if people read this letter, would they come to know you?”
lessons.light: 321 Light: The purpose of marriage isn’t just to build a “good family,” but to build a household that belongs to God and let Jesus receive all the glory. The self-ruled home wants people to see how good it is; the self-emptied home lets people see how good Jesus is. Change from the inside out will in time bring change to our relationships and our ministry.
lessons.jesus: Jesus went to stay at Zacchaeus’s house, and that day his whole household was changed. Jesus said: “Today, salvation has come to this house” (Luke 19:9). No home Jesus enters stays the same. When we invite Jesus to reign in our home, our home too will become a place where others see salvation.
lessons.pray: Holy Spirit, giver of life, write on the pages of our hearts yourself. May our home be a letter from Christ, letting people see not our goodness but the goodness of Jesus. In our imperfection, show your grace; in our everyday life, let people come to know you. Amen.
teach: In Paul’s day, a preacher arriving in a new place often carried a letter of recommendation to prove he could be trusted. Some questioned Paul because he had no such letter, but Paul said: “You are our letter, written in our hearts, known and read by all men” (2 Corinthians 3:2). The changed lives of believers were the best letter of recommendation.

Paul goes on: “you are a letter of Christ” (2 Corinthians 3:3), a letter “written not with ink, but with the Spirit of the living God” (2 Corinthians 3:3). Our home is a letter too. Our children are reading it, our neighbors are reading it, our coworkers, relatives, and friends are reading it. They may not read the Bible, but they read us every day: how we make up after a fight, how we hold each other up when we’re weak.

This doesn’t mean we have to pretend to be perfect. In a real letter, what moves people most is often how God works in the midst of imperfection: a home that once lived in cold silence learning to apologize, a couple who were once worn out praying together again. Let the Holy Spirit write this letter; all we need to do is hand him the pages of our hearts every day. Then what people read in us isn’t how good we are, but how good Christ is.
q: If our family’s life this week were written up as a letter, what words would appear most often?
In front of my family, children, relatives, and friends, what about Christ do I most hope they will read in me?
talk: What do you think our relatives, children, or neighbors are most likely to read in our marriage?
Is there someone we’d like to bless together with our lives, so that they can see Christ?
acts: Today, in front of your family or children, say a word of thanks or affirmation to your spouse
If there’s been conflict lately, take the first step to make peace today, so your family can see what reconciliation looks like
Pray for a relative or friend you’d like to bless
lessons.noon: “you are a letter of Christ” — Lord, right now write your love in my life.

lessons.title: From the Temporary to the Eternal
lessons.theme: Earthly marriage will end, but the eternity it points to never will

v: Therefore we don’t faint, but though our outward person is decaying, yet our inward person is renewed day by day.
For our light affliction, which is for the moment, works for us more and more exceedingly an eternal weight of glory,
while we don’t look at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen. For the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal.
For in the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like God’s angels in heaven.

lessons.still: Look back over this month: marriage was established by God, your spouse is God’s gift, your covenant was made before God, and marriage points to Christ. Now quietly lift your eyes and tell the Lord: “Lord, let me see today’s marriage with eternity in view.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: From earth to heaven, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly. When our eyes are on the temporary, we easily keep score and lose heart; when our eyes are on the eternal, we can endure and hope. Our home is a home on earth getting ready to welcome the Bridegroom.
lessons.jesus: Jesus told his disciples: “I am going to prepare a place for you” (John 14:2). In the wedding customs of the time, a newly betrothed bridegroom would go back to prepare a home, then return for his bride when the time came. Jesus is that faithful Bridegroom. He promised, “I will come again and will receive you to myself” (John 14:3). This is the ultimate hope of our marriage.
lessons.pray: Eternal Lord, thank you for showing us that earthly marriage is a shadow pointing to you. Help us look not only at what is seen right in front of us, but at what is eternal; and in today’s small details and difficulties, keep us walking toward you together. May our home be a home waiting for the Bridegroom, until you come again. Amen.
teach: No one decorates an airport departure lounge as if it were home, because they know they’re about to leave. But no one trashes the lounge or picks fights with the people around them either, because they’re traveling together. Jesus said: “in the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage” (Matthew 22:30). Earthly marriage has a beginning and an end; it is a companion for the journey, not the final destination.

This doesn’t diminish marriage; it makes marriage even more precious. If marriage is a picture pointing to Christ and the church, then when the real wedding feast comes, the picture will have fulfilled its purpose. Paul says: “the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal” (2 Corinthians 4:18). The pain in marriage is real, but seen from eternity, it is “our light affliction, which is for the moment” (2 Corinthians 4:17).

Looking at marriage from a temporary point of view, we ask: “Am I happy right now?” Looking from an eternal point of view, we ask: “Are we moving toward Christ together?” This month we’ve traveled from Genesis to Ephesians and seen that God is the designer of marriage. God designed it, joined it, witnesses it, and in the end will use it to point to the wedding feast of the Lamb. Let’s carry this eternal perspective into every week ahead.
q: The marriage problem that has troubled me most lately: how heavy will it seem ten years from now, or in eternity?
Of this month’s lessons, which idea has most changed how I see marriage?
talk: If our marriage is a journey toward Christ together, where do you think we are on the road right now?
Over this past month, what changes have you seen in me? I want to tell you what I’ve seen in you, too.
acts: Tell your spouse: “Thank you for walking toward Jesus with me.”
Write down one thing God did in your marriage this month
Pray together, entrusting next month’s lessons to the Lord
lessons.noon: “the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal” — Lord, right now let me see my home with eternal eyes.

5.title: The First Couple’s Breakdown: The Root of Self on the Throne

mem.t: doing nothing through rivalry or through conceit, but in humility, each counting others better than himself;

date.t: The Night We Take Off the Leaves
s: Find a quiet, uninterrupted stretch of time, put your phones in another room, and read Genesis 3:7–13 together.
Each write down the “fig leaf” you use most often (for example: silence, busyness, saying “I’m fine”). Take turns reading it aloud; the other responds only with: “Thank you for letting me see.”
Take turns finishing this sentence: “In our marriage, the part I’m willing to own as mine is...” The other adds nothing and makes no comment.
Hold hands and read Philippians 2:3 aloud together, then pray for each other: “Lord, please cover him/her, and cover our home.”

lessons.title: The Serpent’s Whisper: Wanting to Be God
lessons.theme: The root of self on the throne is wanting to leave our rightful place and be God ourselves

v: Now the serpent was more subtle than any animal of the field which the LORD God had made. He said to the woman, “Has God really said, ‘You shall not eat of any tree of the garden’?”
The woman said to the serpent, “We may eat fruit from the trees of the garden,
but not the fruit of the tree which is in the middle of the garden. God has said, ‘You shall not eat of it. You shall not touch it, lest you die.’”
The serpent said to the woman, “You won’t really die,
for God knows that in the day you eat it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil.”

When the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes, and that the tree was to be desired to make one wise, she took some of its fruit, and ate. Then she gave some to her husband with her, and he ate it, too.

lessons.still: Be still and notice which voice is loudest in your heart right now. Tell the Lord: “Lord, among all these voices, I want to listen to yours first.” Gently lay all of today’s doubts and discontent before him.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Pride means leaving our rightful place, grabbing for power, and wanting to take God’s place. Every tug-of-war between husband and wife over “I get the final say” is an echo of that bite of fruit in Eden. To return to our rightful place is to admit that the standard of good and evil belongs to God, not to me. Let people be people, and let God be God.
