lessons.jesus: The tempter came to Jesus too, provoking him to prove himself: “If you are the Son of God...” (Matthew 4:3). But Jesus answered: “Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds out of God’s mouth” (Matthew 4:4). The first Adam reached out and grabbed; the last Adam trusted and obeyed. Jesus shows us that victory begins with believing God’s word.
lessons.pray: Heavenly Father, you are a generous God; you have given us far more than we lack. We admit that we often want to decide for ourselves what’s right and wrong, and that in our home we have sat in your seat. Forgive us. Help us step down from the throne and return to our rightful place. Let your word be the standard for our home, and reign among us. In the name of the Lord Jesus, amen.
teach: Imagine a couple living in a house that lacks nothing, with just one drawer they’ve been told not to open. One day someone whispers in their ear: “He won’t let you open it because he’s afraid you’ll know more than he does.” From that moment on, they can no longer see anything good in the whole house; all they can see is that drawer. This is how the tragedy of Genesis 3 began.

The serpent’s first words were: “Has God really said, ‘You shall not eat of any tree of the garden’?” (Genesis 3:1). God had actually said they could eat from every tree in the garden except one; the serpent twisted a generous God into a stingy one. Then he spoke the real temptation: “you will be like God, knowing good and evil” (Genesis 3:5). This wasn’t just about craving a snack. It was wanting to decide for themselves what is good and what is evil: leaving their rightful place as creatures and becoming God themselves.

This is the root of self on the throne: making myself the center, wanting to be master and king. The text also says: “Then she gave some to her husband with her, and he ate it, too” (Genesis 3:6). Adam was right there, yet he said nothing. On the surface, conflicts in marriage are about chores, money, or children; dig deeper and it’s often the same issue: who gets the final say? When I insist that “my standard is the standard of good and evil,” I am actually sitting in God’s seat. Healing in marriage begins when I step down and let God be God.
q: In which recent matter at home has my heart really been saying, “My way is the right way”?
Is some voice of doubt, about God or about my spouse, making me see only “that drawer” and miss the good things God has already given?
talk: In our home, which area most easily turns into a tug-of-war over “who gets the final say”? Let’s just describe the situation without criticizing each other.
Name one good thing God has already given our home that you’re thankful for, so we can turn our eyes together from what we lack to what we have.
acts: Write down three good things God has already given your home
When you disagree, first say: “Let’s ask together what God wants.”
Notice one moment when you think “My way is right,” and hand it to the Lord
lessons.noon: “Has God really said” — Lord, right now I choose to believe your word and not listen to the voice of doubt.

lessons.title: Fig Leaves: The Hiding Marriage
lessons.theme: Sin makes us hide from God and from each other

v: Their eyes were opened, and they both knew that they were naked. They sewed fig leaves together, and made coverings for themselves.
They heard the LORD God’s voice walking in the garden in the cool of the day, and the man and his wife hid themselves from the presence of the LORD God among the trees of the garden.
The LORD God called to the man, and said to him, “Where are you?”
The man said, “I heard your voice in the garden, and I was afraid, because I was naked; so I hid myself.”

lessons.still: Sit quietly for a moment and listen for that gentle call: “Where are you?” (Genesis 3:9). You don’t need to rush to explain, and you don’t need to hide. Just let the Lord see you as you really are right now. He comes to seek, not to shame.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Hiding is the instinct to protect the “self”: afraid of losing face, afraid of being hurt, afraid of losing control. The self-emptied don’t need so many leaves, because their worth doesn’t depend on how others see them; they have been accepted in Christ. When our focus is on Jesus, we find the courage to be seen.
lessons.jesus: Zacchaeus climbed a sycamore tree and hid among the branches to watch. But Jesus stopped beneath the tree and called him by name: “Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, for today I must stay at your house” (Luke 19:5). Jesus didn’t expose his sin first; he accepted him as a person first. Only someone who knows he is accepted dares to come down from the tree.
lessons.pray: Lord who calls us, thank you for not waiting until we got better before coming to find us. We admit that we often cover ourselves with busyness, silence, and excuses, and that we have built walls between us. Give us courage to step out of the trees and stand unafraid before you; and make our home a place where we can safely be seen by each other. Amen.
teach: After they ate the fruit, their eyes were indeed opened, but not to see God. Instead, “they both knew that they were naked. They sewed fig leaves together, and made coverings for themselves” (Genesis 3:7). Before this, nakedness had been an intimacy without fear; after this, it became a shame that needed covering. The very first thing the first couple did after sinning was to put a layer of covering between themselves.

Couples today have all kinds of fig leaves too: busyness to cover distance, jokes to cover hurt, “I’m fine” to cover disappointment, phones to cover conversations we don’t want to have. Leaves can cover things for a while, but they can’t cover the fear in our hearts. Adam said: “I was afraid, because I was naked; so I hid myself” (Genesis 3:10). Behind our hiding there is often the fear that once we’re seen, we won’t be accepted.

But notice that in this story it’s God who takes the initiative: “The LORD God called to the man, and said to him, ‘Where are you?’” (Genesis 3:9). The all-knowing God knew perfectly well where he was; he was inviting him to come out. Intimacy in marriage is restored the same way: not by waiting for my spouse to take off their leaves first, but by answering God’s call myself, stepping out of the trees, and showing my true self to God and to my spouse.
q: What “fig leaf” do I use most often in our marriage: busyness, silence, jokes, or a quick “I’m fine”?
What side of me am I most afraid for my spouse to see? Where does that fear come from?
talk: When do you feel most free to be your real self with me? What was I doing at those times?
What could I do so that you feel even less need to hide from me? Please name one small, specific thing.
acts: Lay down one “leaf”: tell your spouse one real feeling
During meals or conversations, put your phones in another room
Tell your spouse: “You can tell me the truth. I’ll listen well.”
lessons.noon: “Where are you” — Lord, here I am. Right now I stop hiding. Please see me.

lessons.title: Shifting the Blame: From “Us” to “You and Me”
lessons.theme: The self-ruled heart shifts responsibility, and blame turns oneness into opposition

v: God said, “Who told you that you were naked? Have you eaten from the tree that I commanded you not to eat from?”
The man said, “The woman whom you gave to be with me, she gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate it.”
The LORD God said to the woman, “What have you done?” The woman said, “The serpent deceived me, and I ate.”

lessons.still: Open your hands and rest them on your knees, as if laying down every finger pointed at someone else. Quietly tell the Lord: “Lord, today I won’t start by asking what others did wrong. I’ll listen first to what you say to me.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Shifting blame is the most common face of self on the throne: protecting my image matters more than repairing the relationship. Pride against pride leaves both sides wounded; when one person is the first to say “I was wrong,” humility draws out humility. People matter more than tasks; the relationship matters more than winning.
lessons.jesus: Adam pushed the blame onto his wife, but Jesus took on himself sin that wasn’t his. As he was nailed to the cross, he made no accusation; instead he prayed: “Father, forgive them, for they don’t know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34). The last Adam didn’t shift the blame; he carried it.
lessons.pray: Lord, we admit that we are quick to see each other’s faults and slow to admit our own. Forgive our hearts that shift blame and accuse, and forgive us for even complaining about the spouse you gave us. In every conflict, help us find our own part first and bravely say “I was wrong,” so that our home turns from opponents back into partners. Amen.
teach: God asked Adam a simple question: did you eat? But Adam’s answer took the long way around: “The woman whom you gave to be with me, she gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate it” (Genesis 3:12). In one sentence he blamed two parties: the woman, and the God who “gave” her to him. Eve went on: “The serpent deceived me, and I ate” (Genesis 3:13). Responsibility was like a hot potato, tossed to the next person in line.

Notice how the way Adam refers to his wife changes. Not long before, he had joyfully said she was “bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh” (Genesis 2:23); now she has become “The woman whom you gave to be with me” (Genesis 3:12). Sin turned “us” into “you” and “me,” and oneness into opposition. Shifting blame is like pressing a split button in marriage: every time we say “This is all your fault,” we go from being on the same team to being opponents.

Many couples’ arguments are really contests over who is less wrong. But even when my spouse truly is in the wrong, my response is still my responsibility. Adam could perhaps say that Eve ate first, but that bite was his own. Change begins with me: not “You change first, then I will,” but “Lord, first let me see my part.” Owning my part is the first brick in rebuilding oneness.
q: In our most recent conflict, was what I most wanted to say “It’s all because you...”? What was my part in that situation?
Am I, like Adam, also pushing my discontent onto God: “You’re the one who gave me a spouse like this”?
talk: Think of a small conflict between us (not the most painful one), and each say only: “In that situation, my part was...” The other just listens and adds nothing.
When you feel blamed by me, which of my ways of saying things hurts you most? I’m willing to learn to change.
acts: Change one “It’s all your fault” into “I’m responsible too”
Over some small matter, be the first to say: “I’m sorry, that was my fault.”
Write down one thing you’ve blamed on circumstances or other people that was really yours to own
lessons.noon: “What have you done” — Lord, right now I won’t push this onto others. I own my part.

lessons.title: Seeing Myself First: The Tax Collector’s Prayer
lessons.theme: Seeing my own problems first, instead of fixing my eyes only on my spouse’s

v: “Two men went up into the temple to pray; one was a Pharisee, and the other was a tax collector.
The Pharisee stood and prayed by himself like this: ‘God, I thank you that I am not like the rest of men: extortionists, unrighteous, adulterers, or even like this tax collector.
I fast twice a week. I give tithes of all that I get.’
But the tax collector, standing far away, wouldn’t even lift up his eyes to heaven, but beat his chest, saying, ‘God, be merciful to me, a sinner!’
I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other; for everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but he who humbles himself will be exalted.”
Search me, God, and know my heart. Try me, and know my thoughts.
See if there is any wicked way in me, and lead me in the everlasting way.

lessons.still: Quietly bow your head, like the tax collector standing far off. There’s no need to list your spouse’s faults; simply tell the Lord: “God, search me, and let me see myself.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Moving from looking at others to looking at myself is the turning point from the self-ruled life to the self-emptied life. The self-ruled look at their spouse through a magnifying glass and at themselves through a flattering filter; the self-emptied let the Holy Spirit be their mirror. When I stop being busy trying to change my spouse, God has room to change both of us.
lessons.jesus: When Peter saw the miracle Jesus did, he fell down and said: “Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, Lord” (Luke 5:8). Jesus didn’t leave him. Instead he said, “Don’t be afraid” (Luke 5:10), and called him to go and catch people. Seeing our own unworthiness in Jesus’ presence isn’t the end; it’s the starting point of our calling.
lessons.pray: God who searches the heart, we so often see each other’s problems but can’t see the state of our own hearts. Shine your light on us, so that like the tax collector we are honest and humble before you. And make our home a safe place, where admitting our weaknesses to each other is met with acceptance and support, not ridicule or the dredging up of old wrongs. Amen.
teach: Imagine a mirror that can only reflect other people, never yourself. Many people carry a mirror like that in marriage: they see their spouse’s faults crystal clear, while their own problems always stay blurry. Jesus told this parable precisely “to certain people who were convinced of their own righteousness, and who despised all others” (Luke 18:9). As the Pharisee prayed, his eyes kept drifting sideways: “I am not like the rest of men... or even like this tax collector” (Luke 18:11).

The Pharisee did plenty of things: fasting and giving, both good things. His problem wasn’t his behavior but his comparing. When my heart says “At least I’m not like that,” I’ve turned my spouse into a backdrop to make myself look good. But the tax collector “wouldn’t even lift up his eyes to heaven” and said only: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner!” (Luke 18:13). Jesus said it was this man who went home justified. The renewal of a home also often begins with one person repenting like this.

The psalmist’s prayer is the best mirror: “Search me, God, and know my heart” (Psalm 139:23). Notice that he asks God to search “me,” not “him” or “her.” Seeing my own problems isn’t self-condemnation, because the One who searches me is also the One who will “lead me in the everlasting way” (Psalm 139:24). God shines his light on us in order to heal us.
q: When I think about the problems in our marriage, what comes to mind first: my spouse’s faults, or the places where I need to change?
If the Holy Spirit were to point out one thing in me today, what do I guess it would be?
talk: Each finish this sentence: “One area where I’ve recently realized I need to grow in our marriage is...” Talk only about yourself, not your spouse.
When I admit my problems, how could you respond so that I feel safe? If your spouse can’t join you for now, write down one heartfelt thing you’d like to say to him or her.
acts: When you pray today, pray only for your own change
Notice one moment when you’re comparing yourself with your spouse in your heart, and stop right away
Admit to your spouse one blind spot you’ve only recently noticed
lessons.noon: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner” — Lord, right now I’m not looking at anyone else. I only ask you to have mercy on me.

lessons.title: From Fig Leaves to Garments of Skin
lessons.theme: God himself covers us, so that we can count others better than ourselves

v: I will put hostility between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring. He will bruise your head, and you will bruise his heel.”
The LORD God made garments of animal skins for Adam and for his wife, and clothed them.
doing nothing through rivalry or through conceit, but in humility, each counting others better than himself;
each of you not just looking to his own things, but each of you also to the things of others.

lessons.still: Looking back over this week, you’ve seen your own grasping, hiding, and blame-shifting. Now don’t stay there. Quietly lift your head, look to the God who made clothes for people with his own hands, and tell him: “Lord, thank you for covering me.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Trying to deal with self on the throne in our own strength only sews more leaves; only through the gospel can we move from the self-ruled life to the self-emptied life. Jesus’ death takes away my sin; Jesus’ resurrection gives me new life. Change your mindset and your life will change: I no longer need to win, because I am already loved.
lessons.jesus: Jesus told the parable of the prodigal son: “while he was still far off, his father saw him” (Luke 15:20) and ran to embrace him, then ordered: “Bring out the best robe and put it on him” (Luke 15:22). Jesus shows us the heart of the Father: he doesn’t wait for us to cover ourselves before accepting us; he himself puts the robe on the one who comes home.
lessons.pray: Father of grace, thank you that when we failed, you didn’t cast us off but covered us with your own hands. Thank you, Lord Jesus, for laying down your life for us, so that we no longer need to prove ourselves. Help us to be humble in heart and count each other better than ourselves, and to cover each other with love just as you have covered us. Amen.
teach: Genesis 3 doesn’t end with judgment; it ends with grace. Even while pronouncing the curse, God already promised: “between your offspring and her offspring. He will bruise your head” (Genesis 3:15). This is the Bible’s first announcement that a Savior would come. Then, “The LORD God made garments of animal skins for Adam and for his wife, and clothed them” (Genesis 3:21). The leaves people sew for themselves wither; only the clothes God makes with his own hands can truly cover.

Garments of skin meant that a life paid the price for them. This is a shadow of the gospel: Jesus’ death dealt with both our sinful nature and our sinful acts, and Jesus’ resurrection gives new life. We no longer need our own leaves to prove we’re right, because in Christ we have already been accepted. Only a person covered by God is free from constantly protecting themselves and trying to win every argument in marriage.

This is the power of this week’s memory verse: “in humility, each counting others better than himself” (Philippians 2:3). Counting others better than ourselves doesn’t mean pretending we’re terrible; it means that because my worth is already secure in God, I have room to value my spouse and help my spouse flourish. “each of you not just looking to his own things, but each of you also to the things of others” (Philippians 2:4). Those whom God has covered learn to cover others too.
q: This week, which form of self on the throne has God shown me most clearly: grasping, hiding, or blame-shifting?
In what area am I still using my own “leaves” to prove myself, instead of resting in God’s acceptance?
talk: Name one way in which you think your spouse is “better than me,” and thank him or her specifically.
What was your biggest discovery this week? Going forward, how would you like me to practice this together with you?
acts: Specifically praise one way in which your spouse is “better than me”
Do one thing for your spouse that he/she needs right now, without expecting anything back
Memorize Philippians 2:3 and read it together tonight
lessons.noon: “in humility, each counting others better than himself” — Lord, right now help me see what is good in my spouse and count him/her better than myself.

6.title: Who Is on the Throne? Pride and Humility

mem.t: But he gives more grace. Therefore it says, “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.”

s: Read John 13:3–15 together, then pause in silence and picture Jesus picking up the towel and bending down.
Prepare a basin of warm water and a towel, and take turns washing each other’s hands (or feet, if you’re willing). As you wash, say: “Thank you. I want to serve you.”
Each name one area at home where you most want to “be king,” then say together: “Lord Jesus, please reign here.”
Read James 4:6 aloud together and bless each other: “May God’s grace flow into your heart, and into our home.”

lessons.title: Did I Build Great Babylon?
lessons.theme: Pride means leaving our rightful place and taking God’s glory for ourselves

v: The king spoke and said, “Is not this great Babylon, which I have built for the royal dwelling place by the might of my power and for the glory of my majesty?”
While the word was in the king’s mouth, a voice came from the sky, saying, “O King Nebuchadnezzar, to you it is spoken: ‘The kingdom has departed from you.

You shall be driven from men, and your dwelling shall be with the animals of the field. You shall be made to eat grass like oxen. Seven times shall pass over you, until you know that the Most High rules in the kingdom of men, and gives it to whomever he will.’”

At the end of the days I, Nebuchadnezzar, lifted up my eyes to heaven, and my understanding returned to me; and I blessed the Most High, and I praised and honored him who lives forever, for his dominion is an everlasting dominion, and his kingdom from generation to generation.
Pride goes before destruction, and an arrogant spirit before a fall.

lessons.still: Take a deep breath, then slowly let it out. Think of everything you hold in your hands: your home, your work, your spouse, your children, your plans. Quietly tell the Lord: “Lord, all of this was given by you. I didn’t build it.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Pride puts me in God’s place; humility lays down power and returns to our rightful place. Let people be people, and let God be God. When I acknowledge that “this home was built by God,” I no longer need to trade my contributions for power, or demand that my spouse bow before my crown.
lessons.jesus: Jesus had all authority, yet he said: “For I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John 6:38). He never fought for glory for himself; he always gave the glory to the Father. Jesus is our example: the more capable we are, the more carefully we should keep to our rightful place.
lessons.pray: King of heaven, we admit that we often treat what you have given as our own achievement, and that we have worn crowns at home that don’t belong to us. Forgive our pride. Help us lift our eyes to heaven and return to our rightful place. This home was built by you, and all the glory belongs to you. Rule and reign in our home. In the name of the Lord Jesus, amen.
teach: King Nebuchadnezzar strolled through his palace, looked out over the city, and said: “Is not this great Babylon, which I have built for the royal dwelling place by the might of my power and for the glory of my majesty?” (Daniel 4:30). One short sentence, and it’s full of “I” and “my.” That is the very essence of pride: treating what God has given as something I earned, and taking God’s glory for myself. Pride isn’t always loud and showy; often it’s just a quiet thought in the heart: “This is all thanks to me.”

At home, pride says similar things: “If I weren’t holding this family together, it would have fallen apart long ago,” “I’m the one who earns the money,” “I’m the one who’s put up with everything all these years.” Some of this may be partly true, but when it becomes my crown, I start demanding that others listen to me, thank me, and obey me. Pride means leaving our rightful place, grabbing for power, and wanting to take God’s place. The result is just as Scripture says: “Pride goes before destruction, and an arrogant spirit before a fall” (Proverbs 16:18).

The king was driven out into the fields to live like an animal. But the story doesn’t end there. When the time was up, he says: “I, Nebuchadnezzar, lifted up my eyes to heaven, and my understanding returned to me” (Daniel 4:34). At what moment did he regain his sanity? At the very moment he lifted his eyes to heaven. When a person looks up and acknowledges that there is a King in heaven, he returns to his rightful place as a human being and becomes truly human again. Humility isn’t putting ourselves down; it’s returning to our proper place.
q: In our home, is there a quiet “This is all thanks to me” in my heart? About what?
Have I ever used what I contribute as a bargaining chip to make my spouse do things my way?
talk: Each say: “There’s one good thing in our home that is really God’s grace, not just my doing.” What is it?
Is there any area at home where, because of my “contributions,” you feel you have to tiptoe around my moods? Please tell me gently; I want to hear it.
acts: Change one “I did this” into “Thank God for enabling me to do this”
Thank your spouse for one contribution you usually take for granted
When you pray, say: “Lord, this home was built by you.”
lessons.noon: “Pride goes before destruction, and an arrogant spirit before a fall” — Lord, right now I lay down my crown. Please reign in my heart.

lessons.title: Biting and Devouring: Pride Provokes Pride
lessons.theme: When pride fights pride, both husband and wife are wounded

v: Pride only breeds quarrels, but wisdom is with people who take advice.
For you, brothers, were called for freedom. Only don’t use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh, but through love be servants to one another.
For the whole law is fulfilled in one word, in this: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.”
But if you bite and devour one another, be careful that you don’t consume one another.

lessons.still: Think back to your most recent argument. There’s no need to replay the details; just feel again the force in your heart that said, “I have to win.” Bring it before the Lord and say: “Lord, please calm the war in my heart.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: When pride fights pride, two “selves” are fighting over the same throne. As soon as one steps down, the throne is free for Jesus to reign. Backing up first isn’t losing your dignity; it’s choosing the relationship. People matter more than tasks; the relationship matters more than winning.
lessons.jesus: When the mother of James and John asked for places of honor for her sons, “When the ten heard it, they were indignant with the two brothers” (Matthew 20:24). One person’s pride instantly stirred up indignation in ten others. Jesus didn’t join the argument. Instead he said: “whoever desires to become great among you shall be your servant” (Matthew 20:26). He ended the rivalry with the rules of his kingdom.
lessons.pray: Lord who gives peace, we admit that we often speak in order to win and dig in to save face, and we end up hurting each other. Forgive us for biting and devouring each other, and set us free from the cycle of pride. Help us be the ones who back up first and serve each other in love, so that our home turns from a battlefield into a safe harbor. Amen.
teach: Picture two cars meeting head-on in a narrow alley, and neither driver will back up. One honks, the other honks louder; one inches forward, the other inches forward too. In the end the two cars are bumper to bumper and nobody can get through. Proverbs captures the scene in a single line: “Pride only breeds quarrels” (Proverbs 13:10). In many couples’ fights, the problem isn’t that the issue is so hard to solve, but that neither person will back up.

Pride has one telling trait: it provokes pride in the other person. If I use a commanding tone, my spouse answers with a defiant tone; if I raise my voice, my spouse raises theirs; if I dredge up old grievances, my spouse dredges up even older ones. Paul says: “But if you bite and devour one another, be careful that you don’t consume one another” (Galatians 5:15). When husband and wife bite each other, there’s never a winner, because the wounds are inflicted on the same body.

The way out Paul gives is this: “through love be servants to one another” (Galatians 5:13). “One another” takes two people, but someone has to go first. The second half of the proverb says: “wisdom is with people who take advice” (Proverbs 13:10). The one who backs up first in that narrow alley isn’t the loser, but the one who lets both of them get home. Pride provokes pride and both lose; humility draws out humility and both win.
q: In our recent arguments, am I usually the one who “honks” first, or the one who “honks louder”?
On what kinds of topics am I least willing to back up first? What am I protecting?
talk: What cycle do we fall into most often when we argue? (For example: one lectures, the other goes silent.) Let’s describe it together without working out who started it.
Next time we’re about to start fighting, what code word could we agree on to remind each other to “back up first”?
acts: When you disagree, start by saying: “You have a point too.”
Agree with your spouse on a code word that means “let’s pause this argument”
When you notice yourself raising your voice, take a deep breath and slow down
lessons.noon: “Pride only breeds quarrels, but wisdom is with people who take advice” — Lord, right now let me be the one who backs up first, not the one who fights.

lessons.title: God Gives Grace to the Humble
lessons.theme: Humility draws out humility, and God’s grace flows into the home

v: But he gives more grace. Therefore it says, “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.”
Be subject therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.
Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you. Cleanse your hands, you sinners. Purify your hearts, you double-minded.
Lament, mourn, and weep. Let your laughter be turned to mourning and your joy to gloom.
Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he will exalt you.

lessons.still: Be still, and picture how water always flows to the lowest place. Tell the Lord: “Lord, I’m willing to lower myself and let your grace flow in.” Before him, you don’t need to hold it all together or prove anything.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Humility is the key to revival. I don’t wait for my spouse to be humble before I am; change begins with me. When I humble myself before the Lord, I’m not losing to my spouse; I’m surrendering to God and letting Jesus reign, and grace begins to flow from me into the whole home.
lessons.jesus: When Jesus came to be baptized, John the Baptist tried to stop him: “I need to be baptized by you, and you come to me?” (Matthew 3:14). But Jesus said: “Allow it now” (Matthew 3:15). When humility meets humility, heaven opens and the Holy Spirit descends. Humility draws out humility, and heaven opens to relationships like that.
lessons.pray: God who gives grace to the humble, we are willing to humble ourselves before you, submit to you, and draw near to you. Remove the pride in our hearts that sets us against you, and let your grace flow like water into our home. Help us lay ourselves down first, so that humility spreads between us, and our home experiences your revival. Amen.
teach: Water never flows uphill; it always runs to the lowest place. God’s grace is the same: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James 4:6). The word “resists” in the original carries the sense of an army drawn up in battle against someone. The proud don’t simply miss out on grace; they put themselves in a position of opposing God. But a humble heart is like low ground, and God’s grace flows into it naturally.

James then lays out the path of humility: first, “Be subject therefore to God,” and then, “Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you” (James 4:7–8). Humility is first toward God, then toward people. Someone who can kneel before God can also take the lower place before their spouse. At home, humility looks very concrete: being the first to apologize, the first to put down the phone and listen, the first to admit, “I don’t know. I need you.”

The most wonderful thing about humility is that it’s contagious. When one spouse lets go first, the other often softens too; when one says, “I was too impatient,” it’s easier for the other to say, “I was wrong too.” Humility draws out humility, and both win. And the promise is sure: “Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he will exalt you” (James 4:10). A home that bows low before the Lord, the Lord himself will lift up. Humility is the key to revival.
q: Before God today, in what matter do I need to humble myself and stop trying to hold it all together?
In our home, which humble words are hardest for me to say: “I’m sorry,” “Thank you,” or “I need you”?
talk: Recall a time when “humility drew out humility” between us: who let go first, and what happened next?
What specific way of showing humility would you most like to see from me? (For example: hearing you out before I speak, apologizing first, asking your opinion first.)
acts: Take the initiative and say to your spouse: “I need you.”
On some small matter, ask your spouse’s opinion before deciding
Bow your head and pray quietly for one minute, handing your day to God
lessons.noon: “Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he will exalt you” — Lord, right now I bow low before you. Let your grace flow into my heart.

lessons.title: Clothed with Humility: Let God Be God
lessons.theme: Letting go of control and entrusting both our spouse and our worries to God

v: Likewise, you younger ones, be subject to the elder. Yes, all of you clothe yourselves with humility and subject yourselves to one another; for “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.”
Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time,
casting all your worries on him, because he cares for you.

For I say through the grace that was given me, to everyone who is among you, not to think of yourself more highly than you ought to think; but to think reasonably, as God has apportioned to each person a measure of faith.

lessons.still: Clench your hands into fists and feel the force of your grip; then slowly open them, palms up. Tell the Lord: “Lord, I let go of my controlling hands, and I place my spouse and my worries into your hands.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Control is another face of self on the throne: on the surface it looks like caring, but underneath it says, “I’m in charge.” When I cast my worries on God, I no longer need to clutch at my spouse. When I let God be God, I’m free to be someone who loves, not someone who manages.
lessons.jesus: A rich young man came to ask the way to eternal life, and “Jesus looking at him loved him” (Mark 10:21), and told him the truth plainly. But the man went away sad. Jesus didn’t chase after him to force him, nor did he lower the standard. Jesus shows us that true love speaks the truth, respects the other person’s choice, and leaves the outcome to the Father.
lessons.pray: Heavenly Father who cares for us, we admit that we often want to control each other because our hearts are full of worries. Today we cast all our worries on you, and place each other under your mighty hand. Teach us to clothe ourselves with humility, submitting to and honoring one another. And if there is anything unsafe between us, give us wisdom and courage to seek help. Amen.
teach: Pride has a common but hard-to-spot form: control. We want to control our spouse’s habits, schedule, spiritual progress, even emotions. Behind control there is often worry: afraid he won’t change, afraid things will get out of hand, afraid the future will go badly. Peter speaks of humility and worry together: first, “Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God” (1 Peter 5:6), then, “casting all your worries on him, because he cares for you” (1 Peter 5:7).

When Peter says, “all of you clothe yourselves with humility” (1 Peter 5:5), the word he uses pictures tying on a servant’s apron. Humility isn’t just a feeling; it’s a garment we put on every day. Paul also reminds us “not to think of yourself more highly than you ought to think” (Romans 12:3). I am not my spouse’s Holy Spirit, nor his or her savior. My rightful place is to love and pray for my spouse; changing my spouse is God’s work.

To let people be people, and let God be God, is to place my spouse back in God’s hands: I do my part, and God does his work. Let it also be said clearly: the passage speaks of all of you who “subject yourselves to one another” (1 Peter 5:5): two people willingly honoring each other in the Lord, never one person controlling the other. If there is physical, verbal, sexual, or financial abuse and control in a marriage, that is not submission, and it is not something endurance can fix. Your safety comes first. Please seek help from a pastor and from professionals as soon as possible.
q: What part of my spouse’s life do I most want to control? Behind that control, what am I really worried about?
Am I trying to be my spouse’s “Holy Spirit” in some area?
talk: When have you felt worn out by me “managing” you? I want to hear it, without defending myself.
Let’s each name one recent worry, and then pray together, handing it over to God.
acts: Write down one thing you want to control, and next to it write “Given to God”
Today, resist the urge, at least once, to correct one of your spouse’s little habits
Name one worry and ask your spouse to pray for you
lessons.noon: “casting all your worries on him, because he cares for you” — Lord, right now I place both my spouse and my worries into your hands.

lessons.title: Picking Up the Towel: What Humility Looks Like
lessons.theme: Only those who know whose they are can bend down to serve

v: Jesus, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he came from God and was going to God,
arose from supper, and laid aside his outer garments. He took a towel and wrapped a towel around his waist.
Then he poured water into the basin, and began to wash the disciples’ feet and to wipe them with the towel that was wrapped around him.
So when he had washed their feet, put his outer garment back on, and sat down again, he said to them, “Do you know what I have done to you?
You call me, ‘Teacher’ and ‘Lord.’ You say so correctly, for so I am.
If I then, the Lord and the Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet.
For I have given you an example, that you should also do as I have done to you.

lessons.still: Imagine the Lord Jesus carrying a basin of water and kneeling in front of you. Will you let him wash your feet? Quietly receive his love, then tell him: “Lord, teach me to love my family like this too.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Humility isn’t low self-worth; it’s knowing our identity in God, so we don’t need to fight for position. Only those who are loved and accepted in Christ are free to bend down. When I let Jesus reign, I can serve in peace; when I let Jesus receive all the glory, I don’t need to grab the credit.
lessons.jesus: Jesus, “having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end” (John 13:1). The feet he washed that night included those of Peter, who would deny him, and of Judas, who would betray him. Jesus’ humility doesn’t pick and choose; his love doesn’t depend on whether others deserve it, but flows from who he is.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for picking up the towel for us, bending down to wash our feet, and even laying down your life for us. Let us stand secure in your love and know who we are, so that we stop fighting over who is greatest. Help us wash each other’s feet at home and serve each other in small things, so that our home reflects your humility and you receive all the glory. Amen.
teach: Before John records the foot-washing, he writes something very important: “Jesus, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he came from God and was going to God” (John 13:3). Then he “arose from supper, and laid aside his outer garments. He took a towel and wrapped a towel around his waist” (John 13:4). Jesus bent down not because he lacked status, but because he knew exactly who he was. Security is the soil in which humility grows.

In that culture, washing feet was the job of the lowest servant. That evening, the disciples were still arguing about who was the greatest, and no one was willing to pick up the towel. It looks a lot like everyday life in many homes: the dishes in the sink, the family member who wakes in the night needing care, the trash that needs taking out. Everyone is waiting for “the person who’s supposed to do it.” But Jesus answered the question of who is greatest with action: the one willing to bend down.

After washing their feet, Jesus said: “If I then, the Lord and the Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet” (John 13:14). Notice: “one another.” The most beautiful picture of humility in marriage isn’t one person forever bending down, but both people picking up the towel. When both are eager to serve, there’s no more need to fight over who’s greatest. This week we’ve seen how pride tears down and how humility builds up; now it’s our turn to pick up the towel.
q: What is the thing at home I’m least willing to “pick up the towel” and do? Why?
In what area do I first need to let Jesus serve me and wash me, so that I have strength to serve my spouse?
talk: This week, when did you feel that I was serving you?
What task in our home could change from “waiting for the other to do it” to “both of us racing to do it”?
acts: Do one household chore you usually wait for your spouse to do
Pour your spouse a glass of water, or prepare a small snack
Say to your spouse: “Let me take care of this one.”
lessons.noon: “you also ought to wash one another’s feet” — Lord Jesus, right now teach me to bend down and serve as you did.

7.title: Denying Ourselves: Taking Up the Cross to Follow the Lord

mem.t: He said to all, “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me.

s: Ahead of time, each think of one activity “my spouse loves but I’m usually less keen on.” Do it together this weekend, with no complaining and no checking the clock.
Swap one household chore the other usually handles. Do it with care, without seeking credit or reminding your spouse what you did.
In the evening, read Luke 9:23 together and take turns saying: “This week, one way I saw you deny yourself for me was... Thank you.”
Lay a hand on each other’s shoulder and pray: “Lord, help us follow you every day, and give ourselves gladly for each other.”

lessons.title: Denying Ourselves: The First Step in Following
lessons.theme: Denying ourselves isn’t losing ourselves; it’s finding life in Jesus

v: He said to all, “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me.
For whoever desires to save his life will lose it, but whoever will lose his life for my sake will save it.
For what does it profit a man if he gains the whole world, and loses or forfeits his own self?

lessons.still: Imagine Jesus walking ahead of you, turning back to say, “Come, follow me.” Be still for a moment and ask yourself: “Today, what am I clutching tightly and unwilling to let go of?” Bring it before him.
lessons.light: 321 Light: We deny ourselves for Jesus and for others, not for ourselves. The self-ruled heart asks, “What’s in it for me?” The one who denies self asks, “Will this let Jesus reign?” Only when we stop making ourselves the center do we truly live as the people God originally made us to be.
lessons.jesus: In the garden of Gethsemane, Jesus was so sorrowful he was close to death. He honestly poured out his struggle to the Father, yet in the end he said: “not my will, but yours, be done” (Luke 22:42). Jesus shows us that self-denial isn’t pretending we have no feelings; it is bringing our real feelings and still choosing to obey the Father.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, you said that anyone who would follow you must deny himself and take up his cross every day. We admit that we often just want to live our own way. Give us strength to lay ourselves down in the small things of each day, not to get something in return, but because we love you. In the places where we let go of ourselves, let us receive the richer life you give. Amen.
teach: Jesus said: “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Luke 9:23). There are three actions here: deny yourself, take up your cross, and follow. Denying ourselves doesn’t mean hating ourselves or having no self; it means saying no to “I’m in charge.” It’s like handing the steering wheel to someone who knows the road better: I’m still in the car, but I’m no longer the one deciding where it goes.

Many English translations add one more word here: take up your cross “daily.” (The WEB text leaves that word out, but the call is plainly to an everyday way of life.) Self-denial isn’t one grand, heroic sacrifice; it’s small choices every day. In marriage, the cross is rarely dramatic. Most often it looks like listening to the same worry one more time, giving up the remote one more time, being the first to back down one more time. These small moments of “not my way” are the cross we take up each day.

Jesus went on: “For whoever desires to save his life will lose it, but whoever will lose his life for my sake will save it” (Luke 9:24). The key words are “for my sake.” We don’t deny ourselves to earn something back from our spouse, but for Jesus. People who cling tightly to their own rights often lose the joy of marriage; those willing to lay themselves down for the Lord and for their spouse find a richer life instead. In the end, denying ourselves isn’t a loss; it’s a gain.
q: At home today, what is the one thing I most want to have “my way”?
Do I often treat self-denial as a deal: I gave in to you, so now you should give in to me?
talk: In our marriage, what “small cross” do you quietly carry every day? I want to understand better how hard it is for you.
How can we remind each other to choose “not my way” in small things, without making the other feel pressured?
acts: In one small matter, choose “not my way”
Don’t remind your spouse of what you gave up for him/her
When you get up in the morning, say: “Lord, today I will follow you.”
lessons.noon: “let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” — Lord Jesus, right now I lay down my own way and follow you.

lessons.title: Not Pleasing Ourselves
lessons.theme: Giving way on preferences and habits is love in its most everyday form

v: Now we who are strong ought to bear the weaknesses of the weak, and not to please ourselves.
Let each one of us please his neighbor for that which is good, to be building him up.
For even Christ didn’t please himself. But, as it is written, “The reproaches of those who reproached you fell on me.”

lessons.still: Think about all your preferences: the flavors you like, the room temperature, your daily rhythm, the pace at which you talk. None of these are sins; they’re all gifts from God. Quietly tell the Lord: “Lord, teach me to put my preferences behind love.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Treating my preferences as the standard is the most everyday form of self on the throne. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. Don’t break the heart of the one beside you over the thermostat setting. When we don’t seek to please ourselves, our home takes on the fragrance of Christ.
lessons.jesus: Jesus sat by the well, tired and thirsty. When the disciples came back with food and urged him to eat, he said: “My food is to do the will of him who sent me and to accomplish his work” (John 4:34). It wasn’t that Jesus didn’t care about his own needs, but that something satisfied him more than satisfying himself: doing the Father’s will and caring for the person in front of him.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for giving us different personalities and preferences. We admit that we often treat our own preferences as the standard and argue over small things. Help us not to please ourselves, but to learn to please and build up each other. In the small everyday ways we give way, may we each feel valued, and may our home carry the fragrance of Christ. Amen.
teach: The most common friction in marriage usually isn’t over matters of right and wrong, but over preferences: what to set the thermostat to, what to have for dinner, whether to go out or stay home on the weekend, which end to squeeze the toothpaste from. None of these have a right answer, yet they’re exactly where two people most easily dig in. That’s because deep down we assume that my preferences are “normal” and yours need correcting. Over time, love gets worn thin by one small tug-of-war after another.

Paul says: “Now we who are strong ought to bear the weaknesses of the weak, and not to please ourselves” (Romans 15:1). He was originally talking about believers’ differing views on food and holy days: in matters that aren’t about right and wrong, let love decide. Then he says: “Let each one of us please his neighbor for that which is good, to be building him up” (Romans 15:2). At home, our nearest neighbor is our spouse.

There’s just one reason: “For even Christ didn’t please himself” (Romans 15:3). This doesn’t mean we must suppress our preferences forever; it means letting our preferences step back behind love. Sometimes I give way to you, sometimes you give way to me, sometimes we find a third way together. What matters is that neither of us treats “I like it this way” as the highest law in the house. Denying ourselves in our preferences is a small thing, yet it tells our spouse most clearly: “You matter more than my habits.”
q: In our home, which “I like it this way” have I unconsciously turned into a house rule?
The last time I gave way to my spouse’s preference, did I do it gladly or resentfully?
talk: Name one small thing you really love that you feel I don’t quite understand, and help me see what it means to you.
In what everyday matter could we try “doing it your way this time”?
acts: Choose one small thing and do it the way your spouse prefers
Ask your spouse: “How would you like to spend this evening?”
Refrain from commenting on one of your spouse’s habits that differs from yours
lessons.noon: “even Christ didn’t please himself” — Lord, right now let me put my preferences behind love.

lessons.title: As Working for the Lord
lessons.theme: Sharing the load of chores and time is a practice of self-denial

v: Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ.
And whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men,
knowing that from the Lord you will receive the reward of the inheritance; for you serve the Lord Christ.

lessons.still: Think of what someone has already done in your home today: a meal cooked, laundry washed, bills paid, rides given. Quietly tell the Lord: “Thank you for all the unseen giving in our home.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Running a home by keeping score only breeds more resentment the more we count; running a home by sharing the load grows sweeter the more we do. The focus isn’t on how much my spouse has done, but on what Jesus sees. People matter more than tasks: housework is meant to give the family rest, not to prove who works harder.
lessons.jesus: The risen Jesus lit a charcoal fire on the shore, cooked fish and bread, and said to the disciples who had toiled all night: “Come and eat breakfast!” (John 21:12). He is the Lord of glory, yet he made breakfast with his own hands for people who were exhausted. Jesus shows us that the greatest love is often hidden in the most ordinary chores.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, you are the Lord of glory, yet you were willing to make breakfast for your disciples. Forgive our hearts that keep score over chores and count up our time. Help us see the burdens on each other’s shoulders and reach out to share them; and let us do every chore as for you, so that ordinary days become worship offered to you. Amen.
teach: Someone once said housework is like a treadmill that never stops: the dishes you wash today become a full sink tomorrow; the clothes you fold today become a pile again the day after. Many couples’ resentment builds up on that treadmill as they silently tally, “I do more than you.” Over time, both feel like they’re the one getting the short end of the stick. Housework itself isn’t the problem; the problem is that we’ve replaced sharing the load with keeping score.

Paul says: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ” (Galatians 6:2). Bearing one another’s burdens isn’t splitting everything fifty-fifty; it’s noticing the weight on the other’s shoulders and reaching out first. In some seasons one spouse is especially busy at work; in others one is especially worn out from caring for children or aging parents. A self-denying view of housework doesn’t ask, “Is this my job?” but “What’s your heaviest burden today?” Time is the same: giving up some of my own rest is often the most practical way to share the load.

The deepest change comes when the One we work for changes: “And whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men” (Colossians 3:23). When I wash the dishes for the Lord, I don’t need my spouse’s praise to keep me going; when I take out the trash for the Lord, ordinary chores become worship. This doesn’t mean one spouse can push everything onto the other; it means both of us treat housework as a gift offered to the Lord.
q: Do I keep a “chore ledger” in my heart? What was I tallying the last time I kept score?
If I did one of tomorrow’s chores “as for the Lord,” how would my attitude be different?
talk: In this season, what’s the heaviest burden on your shoulders (chores, work, caring for family, or something else)? How can I help carry it?
Is there a chore in our home that we could redistribute or do together, to make things a little lighter for both of us?
acts: Take over one chore your spouse usually handles
Tell your spouse: “Thank you for all the things you do that I don’t see.”
Give your spouse thirty minutes to rest properly
lessons.noon: “whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord” — Lord, right now the work in my hands is an offering to you.

lessons.title: A Grain of Wheat Falls into the Earth
lessons.theme: Self-denial is like a seed falling into the ground: only by dying can it bear much fruit

v: Most certainly I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit.
He who loves his life will lose it. He who hates his life in this world will keep it to eternal life.
If anyone serves me, let him follow me. Where I am, there my servant will also be. If anyone serves me, the Father will honor him.

lessons.still: Imagine holding a single grain of wheat in your palm. As long as you hold it, it will only ever be one grain; only when it goes into the soil can it grow into a field of wheat. Tell the Lord: “Lord, I’m willing to place myself in your hands and let you make me fruitful.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: The self-ruled heart tries to preserve itself and remains a single grain; the self-emptied heart is willing to fall into the ground and leaves the fruit to God. Life first, then relationships, then ministry: when my life first falls into the ground at home, God makes our relationship fruitful, and then from our home bears fruit that blesses others.
lessons.jesus: Jesus and his disciples were so busy they had no time even to eat. They went off hoping to rest in a deserted place, but the crowds got there first. “Jesus came out, saw a great multitude, and he had compassion on them” (Mark 6:34). He set aside his own rest and began to teach them. Jesus shows us that giving up our time flows from a heart of compassion.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, you are the grain of wheat that fell into the ground and died, bearing the fruit of life for us. We admit that we often want to protect our time, our plans, and our pride. Give us courage to place ourselves in your hands and to sow seed gladly in our marriage. And when we can’t yet see the fruit, help us trust the season you have set. Amen.
teach: Jesus said: “unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12:24). This is the most beautiful picture of self-denial. A grain of wheat kept in a pretty box can last a long time, but it will always be alone. When it falls into the ground and its husk splits open, it seems to lose itself, but in fact it is becoming much more.

Self-denial in marriage is like that. Setting aside your weekend plans for your spouse seems like a “loss”; spending your after-work time really listening to your spouse seems like a “waste”; adjusting your pace when an opportunity comes along, for the sake of your family’s needs, seems like “getting the short end.” But the time and energy buried in the soil slowly grow into trust, intimacy, and security. Self-denial is never simply losing something; it is sowing seed.

Jesus went on: “If anyone serves me, let him follow me. Where I am, there my servant will also be” (John 12:26). Jesus himself is that grain of wheat; his death bore the fruit of countless saved lives. To follow him is to fall into the ground with him and bear fruit with him. Seeds need time, and fruit doesn’t show up the same day; self-denial in marriage also means waiting for God’s season.
q: What am I gripping tightly right now, unwilling to let it “fall into the ground”: my time, my plans, or my pride?
Because I haven’t seen any fruit yet, do I doubt that my self-denial is doing any good?
talk: Looking back over our marriage, when did something you gave up later bear good fruit? I want to thank you.
This week, what time could each of us “plant” in the other?
acts: Take a block of your own time and spend it fully with your spouse
Write down one way you’re willing to “plant” yourself for your family
Thank your spouse for something he/she once gave up for the family
lessons.noon: “But if it dies, it bears much fruit” — Lord, right now I’m willing to let go of myself. Make me fruitful.

lessons.title: Following Gladly, Not Grudgingly
lessons.theme: Self-denial flows from the love of Christ: a glad choice, not a forced endurance

v: For the love of Christ compels us; because we judge thus: that one died for all, therefore all died.
He died for all, that those who live should no longer live to themselves, but to him who for their sakes died and rose again.
looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith, who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising its shame, and has sat down at the right hand of the throne of God.

lessons.still: Think back over the things you’ve given up for your spouse this week. Is your heart light right now, or heavy? You don’t need to hide it. Tell the Lord honestly how you feel, and ask him to move you afresh with his love.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Resentment means the “self” is still there, just stepping back for a while and waiting to collect what it’s owed; self-denial means the “self” has been handed over to the Lord, so there’s nothing to collect. When we move from the human point of view to God’s, from the temporary to the eternal, self-denial turns from a chore into the joy of following the Lord.
lessons.jesus: Jesus said: “No one takes it away from me, but I lay it down by myself” (John 10:18). His self-denial wasn’t helpless surrender but love with authority. When his time had not yet come, he avoided danger; when his time came, he walked to the cross willingly. Jesus shows us that self-denial is a clear-eyed, free choice made out of love.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, for the joy set before you, you endured the cross, and your love compels us. Heal the bitterness that has built up in our hearts from resentment, so that our self-denial flows from love rather than from suppression. Keep everyone in our home safe, and give us wisdom to discern and courage to seek help. Let us no longer live for ourselves, but for you. Amen.
teach: Self-denial and resentment can look alike on the outside, but inside they’re completely different. The resentful person says, “Fine, whatever. It’s no use saying anything anyway.” They keep a ledger in their heart, and the more they give in, the more bitter they become. The self-denying person says, “I want to, because I love the Lord and I love you.” There’s no ledger in their heart, and the more they give, the bigger their heart grows. The difference is what drives them: “For the love of Christ compels us” (2 Corinthians 5:14). Not forced, but moved by love.

Jesus endured the cross “for the joy that was set before him” (Hebrews 12:2). He saw not only the suffering in front of him but also the joy ahead. Those who deny themselves also have joy in view: a self more like Christ, a home more united, a reward in eternity. From a temporary point of view, self-denial is a loss; from an eternal point of view, it’s an investment. Christ died for all “that those who live should no longer live to themselves” (2 Corinthians 5:15).

We must also say clearly: self-denial is not enduring abuse. Jesus’ self-denial was a clear-eyed choice. When people tried to throw him off a cliff, “he, passing through the middle of them, went his way” (Luke 4:30). Physical, verbal, sexual, and financial abuse and control are not a cross to bear, and they are not submission; forgiveness does not mean staying in danger. If you are in a situation like this, your safety comes first. Please seek help from a pastor and from professionals as soon as possible. God wants willing love, not wounded silence.
q: Was there a recent time when I “gave in” but actually did it with resentment? Am I still keeping that ledger in my heart?
When has the love of Christ moved me most deeply? How can I return to that love again?
talk: This week, was there something you gave up for me that actually left you feeling resentful? I want to hear about it and find a better way together. If your spouse can’t join you for now, write down what you’d like to say to him or her.
How can we tell when to give way gladly and when to speak up about our needs?
acts: Honestly hand one “resentment ledger” in your heart over to the Lord
Express one real need by saying “I need...”
Tell your spouse: “I want to do this for you, because I love you.”
lessons.noon: “For the love of Christ compels us” — Lord, right now let your love move me, and don’t let resentment bind me.

8.title: No Longer I: Letting Christ Live in Our Home

mem.t: I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself up for me.

s: Prepare a quiet corner. Light a lamp or a candle, and set out your wedding photo or your wedding rings. Begin by reading Galatians 2:20 together, then pray quietly for one minute.
Take turns saying: “Over these eight weeks, God has shown me that the biggest way I live self-ruled is… I am willing to hand it over to the Lord.” The other person simply responds: “I’m with you.”

Face each other, hold hands, and take turns reading these vows aloud (you may begin with your spouse’s name): “Before God, I choose you again. I confess that I have made myself the center, and I ask you to forgive me. From today on, I will no longer live for myself; may Christ live in me. I want Jesus to reign in our home, and I will love you, honor you, and serve you with his love. In good times and hard times, in plenty and in want, in strength and in weakness, I will follow the Lord together with you, all my life, until we see him face to face. This is my covenant before God.”

Pray together, placing this covenant in God’s hands, and bless each other. If your spouse can’t join you for now, you can read the vows alone before the Lord, offering your own “I do” to God first, and pray a blessing over your spouse.

lessons.title: Emptied, Not Erased
lessons.theme: Self-emptying is not losing yourself; it is entering into God’s limitlessness

v: Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus,
who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped,
but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men.
And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross.
Therefore God also highly exalted him, and gave to him the name which is above every name,

lessons.still: Be still for a moment and picture an empty cup set beneath a spring. Tell the Lord: “Lord, I am willing to empty myself, not to become hollow, but to be filled by you.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Self-emptied does not mean empty; it means entering the limitless and living out of the limitless. Those who live self-ruled have only their own little bit; the self-emptied have all of God. To have the mind of Christ Jesus is to let his heart replace mine, so that my limited self lives inside the limitless God.
lessons.jesus: Jesus said, “the Son can do nothing of himself, but what he sees the Father doing” (John 5:19). The Son of God himself says he “can do nothing.” That is self-emptying at its most complete, and precisely because of it, he accomplished all the Father’s work. Jesus shows us that complete dependence on the Father is limitless power.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, you existed in the form of God, yet you emptied yourself, became a servant, and died on the cross for us. We want to have your mind, to stop grasping, and to empty ourselves. Fill us with your limitless life, so that we no longer live within our limited selves but within your abundance. May you be honored as the highest in our home. Amen.
teach: Being “self-emptied” is often misunderstood as wiping yourself out: no personality, no voice, no needs. Yet the most complete self-emptying in the Bible is Jesus, “who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:6–7). He did not stop being God; he simply refused to clutch his rights. Emptying yourself does not mean becoming nothing. It means letting go of grasping.

This is the exact opposite of the Eden scene from Week 5. Adam and Eve were human, yet reached to grasp a place “like God”; Jesus was God, yet did not grasp. Instead he stooped to become human, “becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross” (Philippians 2:8). The first Adam reached out to grab and lost paradise; the last Adam let go and emptied himself, and opened heaven’s door for us.

The story does not end at the cross: “Therefore God also highly exalted him” (Philippians 2:9). This is the mystery of the self-emptied life: the one who let go was lifted to the highest place. Self-emptying is not a zero; it is placing our limited selves into the limitless God. Only an emptied cup can be filled again and again by the spring. The more a husband and wife empty themselves, the more they will experience together God’s abundance, far beyond all they ask or imagine.
q: What misunderstanding or fear do I carry about being “self-emptied”? Am I afraid of losing myself, or of being taken advantage of?
Where am I still treating some right as “a thing to be grasped,” holding on tight and refusing to let go?
talk: In what way do you think I’m becoming more like Jesus? Please give one specific example, and let’s thank God for it together.
If we both emptied ourselves more, how do you imagine our home would be different?
acts: Let go of one “right” you have been insisting on
Pray in the morning: “Lord, empty me and fill me.”
Memorize Philippians 2:5
lessons.noon: “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus” — Lord Jesus, right now let your heart become my heart.

lessons.title: Crucified Together, Raised to New Life
lessons.theme: Through the gospel, the old self has died and Christ lives in me

v: For I through the law died to the law, that I might live to God.

I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself up for me.
We were buried therefore with him through baptism into death, that just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we also might walk in newness of life.
For if we have become united with him in the likeness of his death, we will also be part of his resurrection;
knowing this, that our old man was crucified with him, that the body of sin might be done away with, so that we would no longer be in bondage to sin.

lessons.still: Read slowly: “it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” Pause, then read it again, saying “I” a little more softly and “Christ” a little more strongly.
lessons.light: 321 Light: You cannot fix the self-ruled life by yourself; the harder you try, the more self-ruled you become. Only through the gospel can we become self-emptied. Jesus’ death deals with our sinful nature and deeds; his resurrection gives new life. Change your mindset and your life will change: I am not an old self trying hard to be better, but a new person in Christ.
lessons.jesus: At Lazarus’ tomb, Jesus said to Martha, “I am the resurrection and the life” (John 11:25). Then he called out Lazarus, who had been dead for four days. Jesus shows us that he did not come to improve dead people but to raise them to life. Even love in our home that seems to have died can come alive again in him.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, you love us and gave yourself for us. Thank you that we have been crucified with you and raised with you. We will no longer rely on our own effort to become better; we believe that you live in us. Show newness of life in our home: in the kitchen, in the living room, in every moment we are tempted to lose our temper, let your life be lived out through us. Amen.
teach: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20). This is Paul’s testimony, and it is our memory verse this week. Notice the words “have been.” Being crucified with Christ is not a goal we strive to achieve; it is a fact already accomplished in Christ. Our practice is to believe that fact and live it out every day.

Why is the self-ruled life so hard to get rid of? Because trying to remove “self” by our own effort is just another form of self-rule, like trying to lift yourself off the ground by your own hair. Scripture says, “our old man was crucified with him, that the body of sin might be done away with” (Romans 6:6). Jesus’ death dealt with both our sinful nature and our sinful deeds; and “just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father” (Romans 6:4), Jesus’ resurrection gives us new life. The gospel is the only road to a self-emptied life.

What does this mean for marriage? Picture two old selves getting married: two egos fighting every day over who gets the throne. But when two people renewed by Christ live together, the home holds two lives in which “Christ lives in me.” Paul says we are to “walk in newness of life” (Romans 6:4). Newness of life is not only for church gatherings; it belongs in the kitchen, in the living room, and in every moment when we are about to lose our temper.
q: Have I been trying to get rid of my self-rule by my own effort? How has that gone?
At what specific moment today will I most need to remind myself: “It is no longer I who live”?
talk: Which part of our marriage do you think most needs “newness of life”? Let’s hand it over to the risen Lord together.
Share a moment when you came to faith, or experienced God’s love more deeply. How did God change you then?
acts: Write Galatians 2:20 on a sticky note and put it beside your mirror
When you feel your temper rising, say silently: “Not I, but Christ.”
Tell your spouse: “Thank you. I see Christ in you.”
lessons.noon: “it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” — Lord, live in me right now, and love my family through me.

lessons.title: The Vine and the Branches
lessons.theme: A self-emptied life remains in Christ and bears fruit naturally

v: Remain in me, and I in you. As the branch can’t bear fruit by itself unless it remains in the vine, so neither can you, unless you remain in me.
I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.
If a man doesn’t remain in me, he is thrown out as a branch and is withered; and they gather them, throw them into the fire, and they are burned.
If you remain in me, and my words remain in you, you will ask whatever you desire, and it will be done for you.
“In this my Father is glorified, that you bear much fruit; and so you will be my disciples.

lessons.still: Imagine yourself as a branch, quietly attached to the vine. A branch doesn’t have to strain; it only has to stay connected. Tell the Lord: “Lord, today I won’t rely on my own strength. I just want to remain in you.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Live from the heart by the Spirit, not from the head by yourself. Those living self-ruled think love has to be squeezed out of themselves, so the more they love, the drier they become. The self-emptied know they are branches, and their strength comes from the vine. When our focus is on Jesus and not on ourselves, fruit isn’t forced; it comes naturally.
lessons.jesus: “Early in the morning, while it was still dark, he rose up and went out, and departed into a deserted place, and prayed there” (Mark 1:35). The night before, he had healed many sick people; early the next morning, he went first to his Father. If Jesus, the Son of God, constantly sought fellowship with the Father, how much more do we need it? He shows us that remaining in the Father is the source of all service.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, the true vine, we confess that we often leave you and try to love in our own strength, and we end up weary and dry. Today we choose to remain in you, and let your life flow into our hearts and our home. Make us bear much fruit of the Spirit, let your love flow through us to each other, and let our heavenly Father be glorified through our home. Amen.
teach: A branch never grits its teeth to produce fruit. It does only one thing: it stays attached to the vine. The sap flows in naturally, and the fruit grows naturally. Jesus said, “I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing” (John 15:5). This is not an exaggeration; it is simply true. Apart from the Lord, we can’t keep up even the most basic love for long.

Many couples work very hard at loving, yet the more they love, the more exhausted they become. That is because they are living from the head by themselves, not from the heart by the Spirit. Live from the head and you fret; live from the heart and you find joy. The self-emptied life is not about trying harder but about staying connected: returning to God’s Word every day, handing ourselves over to the Lord in prayer, and letting the Holy Spirit guide every reaction. A branch has only one job: to remain.

Jesus said, “In this my Father is glorified, that you bear much fruit” (John 15:8). The fruit in a marriage is the fruit of the Spirit: love, joy, peace, patience… and that is exactly what we will learn together in the next stage. This is what 920 (my spouse is my most important “2”; practice the “0” of self-emptying; bear the “9”-fold fruit) looks like: we practice the self-emptied life (0) with our spouse, our most important “2,” we remain in the Lord, and the nine fruits of the Spirit (9) grow naturally, and our heavenly Father is glorified through our home.
q: Lately, has my way of loving my spouse looked more like a branch gritting its teeth, or a branch connected to the vine?
Where is my daily time for “remaining in the Lord”? What is crowding it out?
talk: How can we help each other so that we each have time alone with the Lord every day?
When have you felt that the two of us were most deeply “connected to the Lord” together? How could we have more moments like that?
acts: Take five minutes to read Scripture and pray quietly, doing nothing else
Protect an uninterrupted devotional time for your spouse
Before doing something, pray silently: “Lord, I rely on you.”
lessons.noon: “apart from me you can do nothing” — Lord Jesus, right now I stay connected to you and love by your strength.

lessons.title: The Dividing Wall Comes Down
lessons.theme: The cross put the hostility to death; only two self-emptied people can truly become one

v: For he is our peace, who made both one, and broke down the middle wall of separation,
having abolished in his flesh the hostility, the law of commandments contained in ordinances, that he might create in himself one new man of the two, making peace,
and might reconcile them both in one body to God through the cross, having killed the hostility through it.

lessons.still: Consider whether there is an invisible wall between the two of you right now: something left unresolved, a subject neither of you wants to bring up. You don’t need to rush to tear it down. First bring it to the cross and tell the Lord: “Lord, you are our peace.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Only the self-emptied can become one. Two self-ruled people are like two circles with two centers, forever pulling against each other; two self-emptied people share Jesus as one center, and the closer they come to him, the closer they come to each other. When our focus is on Jesus, not on ourselves, not on others, not on our circumstances, the wall will one day fall.
lessons.jesus: Among the twelve disciples Jesus chose were Matthew, who had collected taxes for Rome, and Simon, who belonged to the Zealots. In most people’s eyes, they should have been sworn enemies; at Jesus’ side, they became companions. Jesus shows us that as long as he is at the center, even the two most unlikely people can walk together.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, Prince of Peace, on the cross you put the hostility to death and broke down the dividing wall. We bring every brick between us to your cross. Take away our self-protective hearts, make you our one shared center, and make us one new person in you, living out a testimony of oneness. Amen.
teach: When Paul wrote these words, he was talking about Jews and Gentiles: two groups hostile to each other, with deep, long-standing grievances. Yet Christ “is our peace, who made both one, and broke down the middle wall of separation” (Ephesians 2:14). If even that kind of chasm can be bridged in Christ, then the wall between a husband and wife is not beyond tearing down in him.

The wall between spouses is usually built one brick at a time: a hurt left unspoken, a cold war, a “forget it, I don’t want to talk about it.” Behind every brick is a self trying to protect itself. This wall won’t fall because one side rams it with all their strength. It falls when both bring themselves to the cross, where Christ came to “reconcile them both in one body to God through the cross, having killed the hostility through it” (Ephesians 2:16).

Why do we say only two self-emptied people can become one? Because two self-ruled people can only negotiate terms, draw boundaries, and keep score; at best they coexist peacefully. Only when both let Christ reign do they share a common center. The passage says Christ came to “create in himself one new man of the two” (Ephesians 2:15). Oneness does not mean you become me or I become you. It means we both become more like Christ, and in him become a new “us.”
q: Is there a “brick” between us that I laid with my own hands? What is it?
In this matter, what do I need to lay down at the cross first, so that the wall can come down?
